utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning colleagues from the Defence. Gramsci Di Fazio, Thomas Hannis, and Selma Sakic, together with our Case Manager Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for Mico Stanisic today, Slobodan Cvijetic, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Deirdre Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic, if you are ready to continue your cross-examination. Witness, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We left off yesterday with your explanation of the statistical definition of the term "displaced persons." You also said that it is distinct from the legal definition, and we have finished with that. Could we look at your report for this case, which is an addendum to the Milosevic report, addendum 2M, which is page 38 in both versions. 65 ter 10399. Page 38. Dr. Tabeau, here in the first column you show the total population identified in 1997, and that's 439.601; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 49.019. That is -- oh, yeah, sorry. You are looking at page 37, not 38; right? 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. My mistake. So the total population is 439.601.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Those are all those who registered to vote in the 18 municipalities of the indictment, and everyone originating from these municipalities who registered to vote in a different municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a different or the same, yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. In column 2, you give us the number of the total identified internally displaced persons and refugees, and that is 192.881.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And if I understood your evidence yesterday, you considered as refugees or internally displaced persons all those voters who in 1991 lived in one of the municipalities in this indictment but did not register to vote in 1997 in their own municipality but registered to vote in a different municipality or registered to vote from abroad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that if for 1997 you identified this total number of voters, 439.601 minus 192.881 internally displaced persons and refugees, then the difference between these two numbers would give us people who were not displaced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And perhaps my maths and statistics would be better today. I would say the difference between these two numbers would be 246.720, if you will take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with this: If the difference between the total voters and total IDPs and refugees is 246.720, then you should have taken that number as the ethnic composition in 1997 and compared it with the census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagree, sir. Why? I will explain you. Because this number does not include incomers. The whole point of the change in the ethnic composition, yes, that a number of population moved out. Another number moved in. So this was what we discussed yesterday, that parallel to moving out of non-Serbs from these municipalities there was an inflow of the Serb population into these areas. So looking at the ethnic composition of the nondisplaced persons identified among the voters is biased because it doesn't take into account those new persons who moved into these areas from other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then as far as this first report is concerned, its tables and statistics, et cetera, I have just one more question. If you have two statistical groups, one of which consists only of permanent residents, and that is the population according to the 1991 census, and the second group consists of permanent residents from 1991 plus incomers from 1992 through 1997, would you agree with a me that these two groups are not methodologically comparable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they are perfectly comparable if you think of a non-war situation, peacetime, right, and we have two censuses, say in 1981 and 1991. Between the two censuses population, of course, changes. Why it changes? Because there are new births, because people die, because there is a migration. There is emigration, there is immigration. So that is a dynamic process. Does it prevent us from comparing the ethnic composition of population of 1991 with that of 1991 [sic], not at all. Not at all. And the concept of moving certain ethnic groups from certain territories and replacing ethnic -- the same -- these ethnic groups with other groups actually is -- has some history in the former Yugoslavia. So I think that we have to take into account the incomers as well, because that's the whole point. That's the whole point of the change, that some people must go and some others must come and replace them, and that is what we have showed in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. Regarding your first report and the addendum made for this case, although this section is identical in both, yesterday my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio mentioned the personal number and said he wouldn't discuss it, and then on page 15420 of the transcript, you explained why you had to compare these changes of names and last names and the whole procedure that took you to the final result. And all this was in the context of the fact that unlike in Western countries that would not have been necessary, because every person has their own ID number which features on a variety of documents, and you said it was not the case in the former Yugoslavia where citizens started to receive their ID numbers in the early 1980s, and these numbers were used only in the 1991 census and in just a few other sources. That is approximately what you said. It's not a quote, but the substance is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us and the Trial Chamber what a unique personal ID number of the citizen is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, this number has 13 digits. Seven first digits is the date of birth. The next two digits is the code for the region of birth, and the next three digits is a sequential number, different for men and women, and the last digit is a control digit. It's calculated according to a certain algorithm and show the correctness of the entire number. That's the concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, but if I may add. These last three numbers but one, you said that they were different from -- for men and women. I would like to add that these were numbers born -- for people born on the same day, and for men it was from 000 until 499, and for women it was from 500 to 999; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- let me put it this way: Would you agree with me that the law introducing the unique personal number, the federal law that applied in the whole of the former Yugoslavia, was passed in 1976 and started to be implemented immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, possibly. I don't know exactly the year, but it sounds reasonable what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And under that law, infants born from that year on received a number according to their place of birth, whereas the law also said that people born before that day would receive ID numbers according to their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say -- and under that law, of course it was logical that each citizen had to have an ID number. Now, would you agree with me that this personal ID number, which is called by the acronym JMBG, is to be found in a large number of identity papers, and it follows all the major events in a person's life, birth, marriage, issuance of a health care card, even student's card at university?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's the concept of the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you, but you said that it started only in the early 1980s in the former Bosnia. But if the law was passed in 1976, all of the citizens by 1991 had received that number. It was, after all, a functioning state, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A large number of citizens did have this number, of course, by 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And in 1991, there were also elections in Bosnia, the first democratic elections. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you have access to those electoral lists, those voters registers from 1991 where every voters' unique identity number would be registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't need to. I had the census of 1991. Why would I look for the voters register?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: For example, because you said that you had difficulties in making your report to find in this 1997 OSC list and in the 1991 census those ID numbers, that they were missing some places, that there were mistakes made. Wouldn't it have been easier to match ID numbers in the two lists rather than trace the names, father's name and other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to clarify. I never said I didn't find this number in the census and in the voters list. That is one thing. Second, I was discussing yesterday that JMBG is unavailable from most sources on war deaths. And that is absolutely correct. This is what I stand behind also today. I didn't ever mention that it was -- the voters register, that it did not include the JMBG. On the contrary. Voters register did contain the JMBG. I said yesterday that the voters register of 1997-8, as a matter of fact, was based on the 1991 census. Further, as a matter of fact, the voters to be eligible to vote, it was necessary to fulfil two conditions. One was to be registered in the population census of 1991. And second condition, it was the age. Further, as a matter of fact, we did use the JMBG number in the matching of the records from the census with the records from the voters. We were lucky to have the JMBG in these two sources because these two sources by far are the largest sources we used in our analysis. Without having this number, disregarding how deficient it was, it would be extremely difficult to match these two sources, as a matter of fact, because the voters was a sub-file from the census files. The JMBG actually contained the same deficiencies in the both, in the census and in the voters. So disregarding the deficiencies, it was still possible to use this number and in matching. About 2 million records were matched based on the JMBG only or in addition with information about the names and about the date of birth. So what I said yesterday was we didn't have the choice. We had to look at names in the census because in many sources on that, the JMBG was unavailable. So that was the alternative way of doing matching. But as a matter of fact we did both, matching based on the JMBG and matching based on the names and other personal information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. If I understood you correctly, 2 million were matched based on the ID number and the rest were matched by some other criteria that we will discuss later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 2 million were matched on JMBG plus additional information. So it would be too risky to use exclusively JMBGs. Why? Because, for instance, in the voters register, wives were often registered using the JMBG of the husbands. So on one hand, a majority of JMBGs were linked correctly to the same person, but there were exceptions that -- like with the wives, so we had to look at other criteria including names. JMBG was the crucial element of matching of the census records with the voters register. I also received additional information from OSCE at some point about how they made the lists of eligible voters, and obviously they used the census records for this, including the JMBG, the names, date of birth, address of residence, so all this information that is necessary to validate when a person comes and wants to register to vote. So they had their own records of the eligible voters from the census. The voters were coming, presenting their own IDs, and this information was compared with what that electoral commissions had at the time of registration. That is basically the census data we're talking about when it comes to the voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, if I may pick up on that. In addition to the JMBG, can you tell us how many other criteria did you use in matching various lists with the 1991 census, because to quote from your report, you talk about the difficulties in matching in the absence of the ID number. Names are either differently spelled or a slightly different date of birth is recorded. Therefore, for persons who were not at first matched, we expanded the search by including one or more variables, let's say just the year of birth or one or more initials in addition to the name and surname. Now, how many additional criteria was that, two, three, six?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sir, I can't remember how many. The -- the list of criteria can be very, very long. But I think it is good to point out that the matching process is a multi-step [Realtime transcript read in error "multistate"] process. In every step a criterion is used to identify potential candidate matches. If the criterion is broad, for instance, if I'm using full first name, full father's name, full surname, full date birth -- date of birth, well, it is quite a narrow criterion. And if I obtain a hundred of matches that are identical on first name, father's name, date of birth and perhaps in addition place of birth or place of residence, it is actually quite a good result and I can declare these matches. All candidate matches can be taken as true matches. However, as you pointed out, there are mistakes, spelling mistakes, in the names, or other mistakes in the dates of birth. So in order to compensate for these mistakes, we have to use broader criteria. For instance, we can use full surname, but only initials of the first name and father's name, and instead of the complete date of birth, only year of birth. And again, in this step there will be a number of candidate matches, but because the criterion was broad, there is no certainty that all the candidate matches are the true matches. So these candidate matches need to be inspected visually. So one has to go one by one through all these candidate matches and decide in every case is this the true match or is it a false match. True match will be a match in which there will be a difference in the spelling in the first name and in the father's name, and there might be a little difference in the date of birth, in the month of birth and the date of birth, because people don't remember dates and the reports will be different in different sources. But if there is satisfactory degree of similarity between two records, then this match can be declared as true. But there will be a number of matches, most certainly, that will have to be rejected as false matches, because the differences will be too large to be accepted. So a number of these broad criteria, of course, had to be used because of the differences in spelling; right? And at the date of birth. Well, actually, it wasn't so much the case between the census and the voters. It was much more the case in matching between the census and the sources on deaths or missing persons; right? So -- but at the same time, the numbers of records of the victims are much smaller, so visual inspection, going through all these candidate matches is physically possible. It would be extremely hard if -- if this would have to be done in the context of the census and voters. However, fortunately in this case the JMBG had been extremely helpful in matching. So I can't say the number, exact number of criteria, but much more than three or two or six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Excuse me. A correction to the transcript, please. Page 9, line 18. It said "multistate." "The matching process is a multistate process." The witness said "multistep process." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said there were several criteria for matching. Why is there no matching statistics in the report? Perhaps I can clarify. Since you used several criteria, why did you not show that, say, for the first criterion there were 20 per cent of matches. The next achieved 30 per cent of matching, et cetera, et cetera. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, I -- I could have done this, honestly, but, well -- first of all, we give some matching statistics in terms of the final matching rate. Because of the number of steps taken during the matching, it would be very time-consuming and, yeah, I'm wondering whether it would be physical -- physically feasible to register every single step we have taken when matching records. Actually, we have been matching records for years and years long, and in order to -- to come up with statistics for the Milosevic report it took us five years to complete the matching and the calculation of the statistics. So it could be done, but it is a very time-consuming process for which I did not always have enough resources. Human resources I am meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We have practically moved to your second report about those who went missing. Yesterday we looked at table 2, which is page 10 in both versions, which is 65 ter 10400. Yes. Page 10, 65 ter 10400. I apologise. It must be the 11th page, then. Yes. No, sorry. It was the 10th page. In any case, we need a simple piece of information. You found that there was a total of 12.047 people who were either killed or went missing. Could you have split the category of those who passed away from those who went missing in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I -- I can do this. So if you need these statistics, I can prepare them. I think that this is mainly killed people, but in any case, I can do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In order to prove that -- well, you have certain death records. I do not dispute that. In order to prove that the people on those lists were real people, and in order to ascertain their ethnicity, you used those records to match them against the 1991 census; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And under such matching criteria, you arrived at the number of 10.430 matches; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the difference between the people you believed were the victims, which is 12.047, and the result of your findings of those who appeared in the census, which is 10.430, when we subtract these two numbers the remaining number is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Aleksic please repeat. The interpreter didn't pick up the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, you heard the interpreters maybe. They did not pick up the last number that you referred to. So could you please repeat it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I wasn't paying attention to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So the difference between 12.047 and 10.430 is 1.617.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this to me, please? Those people do not appear on the census, and yet you took them into account. If I understood well, it turns out that after having analysed a number of the victims, you also included those who were in the census as well as those who were not, or perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I included everybody, the whole 12.047 victims. And if I would exclude the unmatched records, that would mean that I assume that these persons are fictitious victims, and I had no reasons to make such assumption. The matching rate was never 100 per cent between our sources, because the sources are deficient in various ways. So if we obtain a matching rate of 80 per cent, 90 per cent of a given source with the census records, it is already a greater matching rate. All sources that we used for the integrated mortality database are sources that cover victims of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we know this because we know what kind of sources were those sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. But when you analysed the ethnic make-up and forcible migration, you only took into account those whom you found in the census, excluding everyone else whom you failed to identify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, sir, because I identified in the census as much as 90 per cent of the victims from the integrated database, this simply means that I may use certain statistical techniques, I'm again referring to the extrapolation based on what I know for the 90 per cent of the matched individuals over the remaining 10 per cent, I may do that. This is what the statistics tell us. This is a procedure that is fully justified. So what I did, for the 90 per cent I had a complete information from the census about the ethnic make-up. So knowing this, the rest -- the remaining 10 per cent was redistributed according to the observed ethnic composition for the matched records. And believe me, sir, it isn't a mistake. It is a common statistical procedure to do these kind of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness. I truly prepared ahead of time for this conversation, but obviously we'll have to bring an expert of our own who will be able to delve into more detail in order to have it explained to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, good morning. My name is Slobodan Cvijetic. I'm counsel for Mr. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the legal profession, I'm afraid I'll have to correct something my learned friend Mr. Aleksic said yesterday when he said that lawyers, and especially attorneys, are poor at math and that was the reason why they decided to study law since this only partially stands. Namely, attorneys are quick to pick up on a single field or area of math. They say that they can add or -- or do sums very well, but division is another matter. It was an attempt at humour. At the outset I wanted to ask you this: Are you familiar with a demographic or statistical maxim which states that the figure indicates precisely what the person toying around with it intended to show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm unfamiliar with this maxim, so I -- and when I make statistics, I make statistics as they should be made, methodologically correct and based on good sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, it is my position that the maxim stands in full. If in a certain area scientific research is based solely upon numbers, math, and statistics, without taking into account a number of other relevant criteria, especially in the area we are dealing with, one may arrive at seemingly valid results which, however, do not offer an appropriate explanation unless further analysis is undertaken. I'll try to sum up or summarise your work. In the Milosevic case, it was your task to process 40 municipalities included in that indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that correct? It should be 47 in the transcript. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forty-seven, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that case, in keeping with the task you were assigned, you studied seven municipalities in detail and provided an explanation that in those seven municipalities, the issue of demographic changes was the most pronounced and the most characteristic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Those seven municipalities can also be found in your addendum you created for the Stanisic and Zupljanin case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. I don't remember exactly which seven were taken in the Milosevic for a more detailed study.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of this case, you dealt with 18 municipalities included in the Stanisic and Zupljanin indictment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, you also included 26 municipalities which are found in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in other words, outside the territory of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- it's possible. I don't remember all the municipalities, but if you say so, I guess you checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. You will agree with me, will you not, that statistical data and demographic conclusions drawn based on demographic changes in population movements grow in quality with the increasing number of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why would it be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Because statistics and demographic changes need not be aimed at ascertaining the total situation in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to have a realistic view of the demographic changes inside Bosnia and Herzegovina, would not have been the correct -- would it not have been the correct approach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I was tasked to make a report that would give statistics in both cases, Milosevic and in this case, that would give statistics that would be fully consistent with the indictment area and indictment time-frame. Indictment area in Milosevic was larger than in this case. In this cases it is 18 municipalities. In the other it was 47. But if you are interested in statistics for the entire country, I do have them. There is no issue. You can have them tomorrow. So it is, sir, not so that the larger area the quality of statistics -- the better the quality of statistics. Even for one single municipality, take Srebrenica, for instance, or Prijedor, the number of the population is so large that most certainly the quality of statistics for a large area like that is -- is fine. It is -- the -- the -- of -- of -- of the data or your sample you're working with matters if it's -- if you work with small samples, but we were not working with small samples. We are working with the census population, voters register. These are huge populations. And the area study -- studied in both reports was defined according to the requirements of each of these cases and has nothing to do with the quality of statistics. In both case the quality was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't think you have answered my question. The problem is in the sample chosen. In the Milosevic case you chose seven municipalities for which you claim were the most affected in terms of demographic changes and ethnic make-up. In that case as well, you also cited a similar explanation you have used just now by saying that you were tasked to do that by the OTP. However, this is not something that you can justify by scientific reasoning, because you participated in that research, and you chose those seven municipalities. Is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, in the Milosevic report, there are a lot of statistics for the entire country, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there is a lot of comparisons in the Milosevic report of the 47 municipalities or 7 municipalities with the statistics for Bosnia and Herzegovina and with every entity, political entity, that is the RS and FBiH. So there is a lot of broader statistics that create a context in which -- within which the statistics for 47 or 7 can be seen. So these -- this -- blaming me that I made biased choices is not justified in this case. Also, in this report I included some statistics for Bosnia and Herzegovina to give some context for the statistics for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, that wider context was not entered in full in this addendum to the report, and -- and it was thrown out yesterday in relation to the Milosevic case, and we simply lack the information necessary to paint that wider context. I will explain further when we get to that topic specifically. What type of demographics do you deal with? What is your speciality, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, please, sir, I would like to draw your attention to Annex B2 of the addendum. The title of this annex is "Comparison of the Stanisic and Zupljanin Case Area with Bosnia and Herzegovina." Here you can find the contextual statistics for Bosnia in this section. Now, going back to the field of demographics I deal with, I deal with general demography, I think, and in particular I was specialised years long in the study of mortality in developed countries, mostly countries of Western Europe, Central Europe, some East European countries, and I studied life expectancy. So it is mortality, generally speaking. Now, the experience from the ten last years from this Tribunal it would be most certainly war demography. This is a new area in demography which is quite different from classical demography of Western countries or classical demography of another type. But that would be the two areas, the study of mortality in developed countries on one hand, and in addition to this, demography of war. I think there's a correction needed in the transcript last line. It was demography of war I said in the end. This is page 19, row 14. Demography of war. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you have worked on war demographics ever since your collaboration with the OTP began. Sorry, I apologise. You deal with war mortality issues since you began working with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only war mortality. If you look at what I have done here in this Tribunal, there is a study of population displacement, internal and external, a lot of reports on that. There would be these two subjects. War mortality and forced migration I would call it, internal and external.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You did not deal with census statistics and the only experience you have in that area is from your days as a student. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you are referring to my participation in a population census in Poland when I was a student, yes, this was the experience I had at that time, and further, I started using individual-level data from the census here in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you published any papers in census statistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, what kind of paper, technical paper? Definitely not. I did not publish any technical papers on the census. I did publish a paper which was discussing the results of a study in which census data was used. I did publish such papers. But is it for you a publication in the census area? I wouldn't know that. I don't know exactly what you mean. Well, I never pretended to be a technical expert in the conduct of census, and I'm just a census -- a user of the census data, which is not unusual for a statistician. You really don't have to have the technical knowledge of -- of the conduct of census in order to be able to use the census data. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, please, there's a mistake in line 14. It should be conduct, not construct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you did not use data from the so-called vital statistics, births, marriages, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most certainly I did use a lot of vital statistics. I -- I am specialised in the study of mortality, which is exclusively based on vital statistics. Death notification records used for compilation of mortality rates, other measures of mortality all come from vital statistics. It is the official death notifications. Unfortunately, in demography, there is little we can do without vital statistics, birth registration, death registration, marriages registration, divorces. It all comes from vital statistics. Only migration is registered in special registers or there are surveys inspecting the migration flows. But the rest, it is all vital statistics, so I do have quite some experience with vital statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, then you did that after the Milosevic case, because you said there you did not deal at all in that area of statistics, vital statistics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we again miss a context here. Well, if you ask me whether I do have experience in technical aspects of collecting information or records of vital -- for vital statistics or the census, my experience is none. I have never worked in an office registering vital events. I've never worked in the statistical office in which I would be processing the census data. So this is a different group of people who do that. So collecting data, processing data, preparing data for -- for the user is one thing, and I do not have this kind of experience because I'm not this kind of technical person. But using the data with the understanding and knowledge of what is the process of data collection, this is me. I am the user. I am the user, and I have 30 years of experience in using demographic sources. So I think I would strongly disagree with you that I miss the necessary knowledge of vital statistical sources, other demographic sources. I'm most definitely well equipped to be an experienced use of these sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you every worked in the field of ethnodemography? And if you would kindly explain to the Trial Chamber exactly what that means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid that ethnodemography is a typically Yugoslav concept. So we don't have in demography ethnodemography as such. We have studies of ethnicity, of ethnic groups, in demography, but ethnodemography, this term only exists in the former Yugoslavia. As anything in demography of the former Yugoslavia has always been around the ethnic composition of the population and growth of the ethnic group, the differences in fertility of the ethnic groups, so that's the ethnodemography. And this is not how we do things in demography. I'm sorry to say this. Ethnicity is just one of many dimensions the population have -- the populations have. Ethnicity -- we can study populations by ethnicity. We can even make projections, population projections to see how the ethnic groups develop in population, but we do the same things with socio-economic status because the differences by socio-economic status are extremely important. And in mortality analysis, socio-economic differences in mortality and life expectancy is an important aspects of the populations. We -- we do use several other dimensions of the population in our studies, but when we speak of demography, we rather speak of demography of Western countries versus demography of developing countries because these two groups of countries are not identical when it comes to sources of information about the population. If you compare a country like Holland with a country in Africa, take Sudan, for instance, and if you think how much information is available here in Holland about the population, any aspect of the population, and for the population of Sudan, so these are two [indiscernible]. So obviously there must be different methods, approaches and sources used in the study of these two different populations. But ethnodemography, we don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Ms. Tabeau, I see a problem there. You came to a region where this ethnodemographic factor or, in other words, study of demography by ethnic group is a very important thing, and you neglected it. You did not deal with it, and you did not apply it to the region where you were working. And I will use practical examples to show you how this reflected on your findings. Let me start with some basic characteristics of ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina to see if you know at least these basic characteristics of ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you know that the Muslim population as an ethnic group is characterised by low mobility in terms of emigration and immigration, high density of population of their areas, the areas where they reside, and a high birth rate, actually higher than any other ethnic group in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of these basic features?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are your theories, Mr. Cvijetic, and as a matter of fact, we should be talking about my report and the results presented in my reports, and you are supposed to challenge me if I made any omissions or things like that, and you are discussing me -- with me your theories. So I would suggest we move to the actual topic of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you just reply. Do you know these basic features or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made a study of fertility of ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Never published, unfortunately, and perhaps I shouldn't even be talking about this because it's my internal product which I didn't share with anybody. But in the census, there is an information about children ever born for every women -- woman. And it's possible to study differences in fertility of ethnic groups. One can do it in many ways. In demography we have two major perspectives. We have a cross-sectional perspective, so we look at fertility in one period of time, or we study fertility in cohort, that is longitudinally. This means that we study number of children born by every women in their reproductive age.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. That is just one aspect of ethnic characteristics. I didn't mean to deal with each one individually until I come to the practical examples showing how that reflected on your report. If I understood your reply, the reply is no. No, you did not deal with it, and you do not know these basic ethnic characteristics. MR. DI FAZIO: I object to the question, if Your Honours please. Although Ms. Tabeau's quite capable of dealing with these questions I must nevertheless object, because it's what exactly is Mr. Cvijetic referring to when he says she doesn't know these basic ethnic characteristics? There's nothing, nothing at all in any of the reports that touches upon the issue of ethnicity other than the way people reported themselves by writing down Muslim, Serb, or Croat in the census taken in 1991, and yesterday she gave evidence, and it's in the reports, that was the sole basis of studying any of these numbers. Nothing about any other study that she may have done on what is referred to as "ethnic characteristics."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may say, well, you said I don't know anything about these issues. I say I am unaware of your theories, and I don't want to be aware of these theories because they are unrelated to the subject of my reports. But it is not correct to assume that I myself haven't studied certain issues like, for instance, fertility or birth rates among the ethnic groups, density of the Muslim population, urban-rural distribution of this population, migration before the 1991 census, these kind of things, because you have no basis to blame me of not having any experience in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well if you have that experience, why haven't you still answered my question about the ethnic characteristics of one ethnic group? And I will later put questions about the other two. MR. DI FAZIO: For the record, if Your Honours please, that's going to meet with objection each and every time. The question of ethnic characteristics is utterly irrelevant to any of these studies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Cvijetic, please move on to another area. It will be pointless going down this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a point to this, and you will see it when I give a practical example, because demography is not just maths and statistics. If you just take maths and statistics, discounting all the other democratic factors, you don't get the correct conclusions. Let's take an sample of four residents, four inhabitants, and according to their self-declaration and gender you get two men and two women. One of the two men has both wives. Both the women as wives, and the other one, the other man, does not have a wife. On average, they're both married, but every night, one of them goes to bed alone because he does not have that statistical wife. I will also point to all the other factors that affect demographic movements in population which must be linked to the mathematical and statistical findings. Mathematical statistics are bone dry and do not give us a real picture of the population. Now, counting the percentage of the population under 18, for instance, is different for different ethnic groups, and that reflected on the maths of Mrs. Tabeau. But since the Trial Chamber wants me to move on, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How and on what basis did you determine ethnicity, nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the census, 1991, question, open-ended question, "What's your ethnicity?"

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you did not use language, religion alongside, and you did not combine these two with the self-declared ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It was a self-perception of every person in the census as reported in the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that census for Bosnia and Herzegovina, 239.845 respondents declared themselves as Yugoslavs. So they have not declared themselves as belonging to any ethnic group, and you placed them in the category of others; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, they did declare themselves as Yugoslavs, not as Serbs, Croats, Muslims, any other ethnicity. They did declare themselves as Yugoslavs. Why Yugoslavs would you assume is no lack of ethnic declaration? Why is that so? Well, I saw, you know, at several occasions that the Serbs would say most of Yugoslavs were the Serbs. The Croats would say, oh, no, no, no. Most of the Yugoslavs were the Croats, and the Muslims, no, no, no, most of them were Muslims. But, as a matter of fact, they did declare themselves as Yugoslavs. It's as good ethnicity as any other. Didn't you think about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, Yugoslav is citizenship. A Serb who declares himself as Yugoslav is still a Serb, but within that -- MR. DI FAZIO: I object, Your Honours. The -- we're entering into a discussion about what it is to be a Yugoslav, and that is utterly irrelevant. Ms. Tabeau has made -- repeatedly made it clear that in terms of ethnicity, she only used what the answer was in the 1991 census and never looked into the question of whether -- what aspects or characteristics a person who wrote down Muslim, Croat, Serb, or Yugoslav had in their mind when they wrote that down, that answer. So to enter and go down that road and to discuss that is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, Yugoslavs are not extraterrestrials. They are Serbs, Croats, Muslims and others who declared themselves as Yugoslavs. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what you say, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I thought -- I thought that Mr. Di Fazio's objection so clearly pointed out the direction which you should be headed that I'm surprised that you're persisting in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain in just one sentence and stop there. The category of Yugoslavs, precisely because of this lack of ethnic declaration, creates a mathematical error in the make-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina and may not be used, cannot be used. And if it's not used, it gives us a corresponding percentage of error in the statistical data.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may make one comment. In statistical publications of the census data by statistical authorities from the region of the former Yugoslavia, Yugoslavs are distinguished as yet another ethnic group along with the Muslims, Croats, and the Serbs, and the remaining ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not repeat what that category consists of. It's already on the record. Your Honours, I think perhaps it's time for the break. I'm about to move to a new area, namely, the sources used by Mrs. Tabeau, and it's quite a large subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, may I just very briefly raise one matter with you. It's not relating to this witness but, rather, to the schedule for the rest of the -- well, today and tomorrow. Unfortunately, we're not proceeding as fast as I thought we might have this morning, and it looks as if we may be using a goodly part of today, and that's really going to cause problems with the next witness. You already know what the situation is with that witness and his commitments on the weekend and how the Prosecution was very anxious to finish him before the weekend because he has to go back for personal reasons. Accordingly, I'm asked to ask you if it is at all possible to arrange not only the extra sitting today which has already been arranged but an extra sitting tomorrow as well. I understand it may be possible and Ms. Korner is anxious that we try and arrange that at all if at all possible so that we can complete the next witness in time for him to go back to his commitment on the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When did you -- when did -- just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you confirm, Mr. Di Fazio, that the witness has to -- is it tomorrow morning that the witness has to leave? MR. DI FAZIO: No, no. He's got a commitment on the weekend, on Saturday. So the situation is that Ms. Korner is very anxious for that witness to start as soon as possible so that all of his testimony can be completed before the weekend, and I think that makes good sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we're at the start of the second session for today. When, as you see things now, do you expect to begin him, to begin his testimony? MR. DI FAZIO: Immediately after this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but in terms of time, when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In other words, how long is your redirect going to be? MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. I'm sorry, I misunderstood you. As things stand at the moment, I have none. And -- yes, none at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, when is 163 -- when does he have to leave The Hague? Do you know? MR. DI FAZIO: Saturday morning, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we're aware of the original estimate of time that your cross-examination was intended to take, but the Chamber's observation is the way the cross-examination has proceeded to date, that it is such that we are requiring you to complete your

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this session, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, the end of the session that we're beginning, which would ordinarily end at 12.05.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, then I shouldn't even begin, because I can't conclude, and if I have opportunity to say this, please hear me out. It is an unnatural pressure that the witness we are discussing be heard by a certain time. This pressure is occurring not for the first time. For the Prosecution, the next witness is much more important than the witness currently on the stand, but they say so only after they have completed their in-chief, and then they put pressure on the Defence to shorten their cross-examination. Now, the witness has to attend a wedding. We deleted one witness from the list to accommodate that. Now we are asked additionally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt you, Mr. Cvijetic. I'm not concerned about the witness to come. The reason for the Chamber requiring you to complete your cross-examination by 12 -- by the end of this session is that in terms of what we would have heard from the witness presently on the stand, there has been no challenge to her methodology or her credibility or competence as an expert witness, and therefore it does not appear to us that the way that cross-examination has proceeded has been within the requirements for relevance, which is the fundamental criterion even for cross-examination. And having regard to the demonstrated path down which you have proceeded so far, that is why we are requiring you to wind up your cross-examination of this witness at the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, the methodology of cross-examination implies also a certain tactic. In that tactic, the punch line comes at the end. All my introductory remarks I will attempt to link up with the specific findings of Mrs. Tabeau at the end when we open up some of her tables. But if you don't make it possible for me to do that, I cannot reach that final goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you indicated yourself that you would need approximately two hours and the Court relied on that. So my best advice is get on with it and let's round this up by the end of this session. You have plenty of time to put the questions that you need, and -- and there is no point in seeking to start out with a number of irrelevant questions just in order to put your final questions in the end. You may as well proceed straightforward and directly to the questions that you really want to put to the witness. So let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will not be able to complete by that time, hence I will go as far as I can and stop then. Our initial assessment was four hours for myself and four hours for my learned friend. When we discussed how to divide our examinations in terms of topics, I suggested that I take over a number of topics he intended to cover, and that's why I -- I need additional time to what we had originally requested. That is why the change. However, we never opposed any such requests made by the OTP, and I am uncertain why that is imposed on us now.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, we arrive at the sources you used. Out of that number sources, if we start with the most relevant up to the least relevant or least reliable from a scientific point of view, would you be able to put them in such an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are speaking of which report?

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: The sources you used for all of your reports. Not a single report but all of your reports that refer to the sources you specified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think major sources I used for the IDPs and refugees report, the census and the voters are of course the essential sources. The rest sources are -- used are contextual so are not my major sources. I didn't use them for -- to produce statistics. And when it comes to the report on victims, I think I used sources that I see as highly valuable, highly valuable and as you certainly remember, there is a table in -- in my report in which the sources are listed and I'm taking you to page -- page 8 in the English version. We discussed this table yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. Please hear me out. If we refer to sources, would you be able to make a list that starts with the most relevant and ends with the least relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All my sources are relevant. It is not that they are irrelevant. They are all relevant. This is what I'm trying to tell you. I said for the IDPs report, census and the voters are my essential sources. Other sources are contextual. And in the report on victims, all my sources are relevant. But obviously, the ICMP records of the DNA identification of Srebrenica victims were not used for this report, whereas they were used for the entire integrated Bosnia database, because Srebrenica is part of it and is not of this case. So that's the -- how to read the relevance of the sources. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, in your report you say that some of those sources are not reliable and that do not -- and that they do not have equal scientific value. In your addendum B5 to the Milosevic case, at page 235 in the B/C/S and 222 in the English -- it is 65 ter 10398. Well, I'll read out. We don't need to wait for it to appear on the screen. You say registering to vote was voluntary, which means that the list of voters is but one of the samples of post-war population, because it excludes those who had not registered to vote, because they were either not interested or because they were ill or too young or too old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I said, and this is true. But at the same time, you must be aware of the fact that there was no next census. There has been no census since 1991 in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So while we know that voters register has certain deficiencies and is incomplete, there is no alternative source that would be complete and covering the entire population that we could have used in this study.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Very well. In the same exhibit, at page 222 in the B/C/S and 208 in the English version, you say that the census itself as the single most important starting point for your research has its deficiencies, but you begin that sentence in the following way: "Due to the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, the data processing procedure of the census information was halted." Ms. Tabeau, this term "the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina," did you coin that term? Is it yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is clearly indicated in that report, Milosevic report, that this particular annex, Annex B3, was written by Nora Selimovic. She's the author of this particular text, and I didn't make any changes in her original report. She was the one who participated in the Republican Census Commission and in the census itself.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Those reports drafted in Sarajevo, in the institute you referred to in your report, as well as those reports based on the survey conducted in Sarajevo are accepted as relevant sources by you. I believe in the Milosevic case, you did say that, nonetheless, these sources were biased.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did accept the report by Nora Selimovic, and I did accept the Sarajevo Household Survey to which you are referring. The survey was conducted in 1994. It is one of the sources I used for the victims report, but I am not recalling I'm calling these sources biased. I'm not blaming Nora Selimovic to be biased. She is the best professional who can give us the opinion about how the technicalities of how the census were done. That is one thing. And Sarajevo Household Survey, it is a survey -- it is a wartime survey, so conducted in mid-1994 by a group of people who just went to see every household living within the front lines and collected reports from these households about all deaths that occurred in their families until the moment of the survey. I don't think there is any bias here. If it is a survey that is meant to be complete, that every household is questioned on these issues, if they would have been selective according -- or acted to a criterion that would be oriented towards one ethnic group and not others, but I don't recall calling them biased. If you could show me this in my reports, I would be grateful. I worked with sources from all sides. I have, for instance, RS Mortality Database that was compiled for us by the statistical office of the Republika Srpska in Banja Luka. I had a long co-operation with Mr. Slavko Sobot, the director of the office, and I accepted all this data as much as I accepted data from the federal authority. So I disagree that I am biased in accepting my sources. I take sources which are most relevant and most reliable. I just work with the best sources available. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours, please, RS is missing from line 10. I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, RS is missing, RS Mortality Database.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, to be fair to you, not even the data you used that were collected by the national security agency of Banja Luka represents anything more than their assessment and information gathered by operative work. Those were not -- that is not information gathered by standard methods when studying populations. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I might -- I have my doubts regarding the method. At some point I discussed the surveys with Mr. Sobot, the director of RS statistics, but he insisted these surveys were run according to formal statistical procedures for conducting the surveys. I can, however, imagine during the wartime not all statistical procedures could be followed because of the war, because of the fighting that was going on, because of the chaos, because of many difficulties. And as I said, the RS sources are contextual. I never used these sources for making my own statistics.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Can it be justified in terms of methodology to compare and merge a methodologically sound source such as a census with sources which, as you yourself say, bear deficiencies -- MR. DI FAZIO: I object, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: -- all the way up to being openly biased. MR. DI FAZIO: The witness has just said that she didn't do that. She just said that she didn't do that. She didn't use the RS sources to draw her conclusions in her reports, all three of them. She looked at them, she looked at what they said, and you can see that in her report, but she just said that she didn't merge them -- sorry, the expression used by Mr. Cvijetic is that she merged them. She says she didn't. She looked at them and she spoke to this guy, this Mr. Sobot, and she provided a report, but she didn't use them in drawing the conclusions in her reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, your question as phrased -- Mr. Di Fazio is correct in his objection, but I think -- if I think I understand what you're getting at, perhaps you need to ask a preliminary question before you rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I thank Mr. Di Fazio for answering my question, hence there's no point in repeating it. I had in mind the methodology approach by which one should not link separate documents of different degrees of reliability. That is the gist of my argument.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Is that methodologically sound and justifiable, Mrs. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By linking you mean just comparing, putting one source on one side, another on other side, and that is wrong, you are saying, because the sources are so extremely uncomparable in terms of methodology. I think what is -- what regards the methodology, as I said, I have my doubts about -- about the methodology, that these surveys by the RS MUP were not conducted, I think, according to the statistical regulations. On the other hand, I know from a statistic authority they were attempted at least to be completed according to statistical regulations. So, okay, there is some doubt about the methodology. Still, the coverage of the sources and the period on which the sources report are relevant. Why don't look at these sources to create some additional information about the time in which I'm interested? I see no problem in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, there is a word that you used that I didn't get, and neither did the reporter. It's still the something of the sources.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The coverage, territorial coverage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Territorial coverage and the time periods are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'm comparing what is comparable from this point of view. I am not comparing things that are completely different and uncomparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau -- Ms. Tabeau, if one distributes 85 questionnaire -- 85.000 questionnaires in Sarajevo in order to try and ascertain the number of war victims, and if such a survey is conducted by Muslims, and if the results of that survey are explained by saying "killed during enemy aggression," "killed by enemy forces," "killed by aggressor sniper shooter," could such findings or results be considered biased? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are referring killed during enemy aggression. These are the terms from where? From the questionnaire, from the reports these authors made about these results or I used the terms? As far as I recall, I never used these terms in any of my report.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: I have shown the page of your report in which you quote the report which states: "Due to the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina, the data was not analysed," et cetera. So you even accepted the terminology of that report. Please just answer my question. Is such data collected in that way biased? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the page you are referring to relates to the census, and it was written by Nora Selimovic. If there is another page in which these kind of terms are used in my reports, then please show this page to me. That is one thing. Okay? Once we clarify this, then I can tell you that -- give you the answer then. As far as I remember, I myself never used this kind of terms in any report of mine.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, in the Milosevic case when you were assessing the quality of sources received by the Sarajevo institute, at page 27162, you openly stated that the sources were biased. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are referring to Milosevic case IDPs report or another report from Milosevic case? I did have some reports on Sarajevo in Milosevic case, that is correct. But if you are referring to these reports, then please tell me which report was that.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you commented upon the scientific quality of the sources received from Sarajevo. That's the topic of our discussion, and on the page I referred you to, you -- you termed them as biased. Do you recall that? MR. DI FAZIO: The witness has already said that she's got trouble answering that question because she doesn't know what report's being referred to. And the whole process would be vastly simplified if the passage from the transcript was simply read to her and put to her. Then she knows exactly what's going on and she can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Would it assist you, Ms. Tabeau, to have your reply from the Milosevic case read out to you? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, of course. This is what I am still waiting for. I need the source in order to be able to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will ask my assistant to read out in English, and I'd like to ask the interpreters to interpret it into the other languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SAVIC
utterances.text: "All right. But in your opinion, since you're a demographer and since you're involved in scientific work, do you think that this approach is partial? "A. Well, I can make an assessment of the scientific quality of the questionnaire and how the survey was conducted on the basis of what I know about the survey and the questionnaire, and indeed this is one thing. I cannot say whether it was partial or impartial. I can say that the material was probably biased a little bit towards more frequently counting Muslim casualties than casualties from other ethnic groups. Why? Because people who conducted the survey were engaged in the survey -- survey were mainly the Bosnian Muslims from Sarajevo. So therefore, they could have had a little bit easier access to respondents of the same ethnicity than as to respondents from other ethnic groups." MR. DI FAZIO: Can I have the page number of the transcript, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SAVIC
utterances.text: Page 27162, Milosevic case. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I know what this passage relates to. It is related to the Sarajevo report that I made for the Milosevic case. It is about the Sarajevo Household Survey of 1994 that I already mentioned, and it -- this survey indeed was run by Bosniaks, who most definitely had the easiest access to the Bosniak families. But the survey as such was claimed by the authors to be indiscriminative in the sense that every household who lived within the area of the front lines was covered. This is one thing. I said indeed slightly biased towards Bosniak or Muslim victims and it is probably the case. But if you think that in the RS Mortality Database there are all Bosniaks and no Serbs, no. It is the other way around. These are mainly Serb victims reported there. So that's the whole thing about sources on war victims. Sources are biased this way or another, and therefore it is very important -- important to work with many sources, to combine the sources and to eliminate the bias and to understand that there is a bias. If I have used the Sarajevo Household Survey as the only source, exclusively source in the integrated mortality database of Sarajevo, then I would be wrong, but I didn't. I had several other sources that covered Sarajevo as well, and so was it in the Sarajevo report that I presented in the Milosevic case. It was a study based on eight large sources on war victims. So the point is, yes, I'm aware, sources are biased. And we have to do our best to understand this bias, identify the bias, and be able to deal with it in order to come up with unbiased statistics. And I'm absolutely truly convinced that the statistics that they obtained from the integrated database have no ethnic bias as such. Why? Because of the many sources we used that covered all ethnic groups, all territories, all major incidents. It's all very well covered. So I can assure you there is no ethnic bias in this database.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you will agree with me, since you touched upon a topic that I meant to deal with at the end, which is the issue of victims and mortality, that in that area, the grey area not backed by solid data is the largest, because we have in that area the most extreme research including 500.000 victims down to a -- down to the figure of 80 or 90.000 victims that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are incorrect. 500.000 victims have never been mentioned by any author for the war of Bosnia -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There have been various estimates. The highest, I believe, was 340.000 victims. The lowest was 25.000. The minimum number we presented, 90.000, is actually -- yeah, not definitely the highest one and not definitely the lowest one. It is somewhere there in between. But what is important about our number, 90.000, or the more complete estimate including the estimated undercount, which gives us 104.000 victims approximately, this number actually is also supported by results of a totally different group of people, people who operate in the former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Sarajevo. I'm speaking of Mr. Mirsad Tokaca and his centre, documentation and research centre in Sarajevo. They established a database on war victims in Bosnia and Herzegovina completely independently from the work we've been doing here, and these victims are also documented with personal details, names and details as well. And he obtained a number approximately 99.000 victims. So it's the same class. It is the same class of result; right? So I would think of these two as the two most serious attempts to estimate victims of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I could -- I could go on explaining why, and I could say things about every single of the estimates presented so far, but I think we don't have time for this, so I will finish here.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: You obviously do have time, whilst, on the other hand, I don't. I will accept the range you specified. In that case, you have to agree with me that in the area of mortality, the figures were played with the most, and I refer you pack to the maxim I mentioned at the beginning: If one wants a certain figure, that figure will be ascribed the importance one wishes to attach to it. However, Ms. Tabeau, you will agree with me that even within the range you referred to, the game goes on, in the sense of how many people were killed as soldiers and how many were civilians. If we add to that the natural, undisputed fact that there were natural deaths as well in that period, there is a possibility for manipulation even with the figure of 90.000. Is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the 90.000 I produced is well documented. I exactly know and wrote about it, what sources were used, what methodology was used. I -- I've been completely transparent about the method, unlike many other authors about their results. If there is room for manipulation, then it is not research anymore. It is the manipulation, and this is something I'm not interested in. We don't need that. We don't want manipulation. We want solid research that can be discussed, about which we can be open, and others can express their opinions about this research. This is what we need, and this is what I have been doing many, many years. I think that the 100.000 of victims that have been produced for Bosnia by my group and also by group of Mr. Tokaca, I think are good numbers. If -- if there are people who want manipulate, this is their problem, but the victims don't need that, the families of the victims. We don't need that. Nobody needs manipulation. That is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Is there an institution in existence at this point in time which can firmly stand behind a number of those killed and the number of those who died due to natural causes, as well as an exact figure of those who perished in combat operations, as well as the number of civilians? MR. DI FAZIO: I object to the question, if Your Honours please. It's now entering the realm of repetition, and it's -- it's, with respect, not particularly coherent. First of all, there's a question about an institution in existence which can firmly stand behind a number of those killed. The witness has just told you and repeated it twice in several answers that she's made an assessment of people killed in Bosnia that the OTP demographics unit has. She stands by it, you've heard her say that. She also mentioned another, this other organisation in Bosnia headed by this Mr. Tokaca. And finally, the witness in her reports said nothing about any study into people dying of natural causes. If Mr. Cvijetic wants to demonstrate that somehow the studies are flawed because there is no study of people who died from natural causes, well, he can do that, but he must proceed to that topic, not the way the question is framed at the moment, which touches upon institutions, whether they stand behind their figures, and whether or not natural causes are discussed by those institutions or this witness. It's incoherent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please try again, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the question was clear. Mr. Di Fazio stood for no other reason but to waste my time and did not assist me in reaching any answers.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: My question was: Is there an institution which can firmly stand behind the four figures I just referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what would be the relevance of that question, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it includes an entire chapter of Ms. Tabeau's work which deals with war victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I still don't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is great relevance in the number of those who got killed in combat participating in the war and those who got killed as civilians, because the latter are a protected category that we deal with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Why don't you ask about that then instead of asking about institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a substantial issue whether that information exists and from whom we can get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, I will not use your precious time further, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is no time. It's already been used up.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, I'm not getting an answer, whatever I ask. I'll move to my next question. My colleague discussed with you the deficiencies in ID numbers, and you've already answered that. Do you know that these inaccuracies in ID numbers amount to 30 to 40 per cent? Do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall these exact per cent. However, there are two things. There is the date of birth, seven first digits, and that is the actual maticni broj, that is the remaining digits of the 13. When it comes to the date of birth, which was very important for us --

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: You have answered that. I just want to know if you had the information about the inaccuracies that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I'm trying to tell you. I am aware of inaccuracies, and they are related to the actual maticni broj, not to the date of birth that is essential for us in our work.
