So the other part, the maticni broj, the actual maticni broj that begins with the record of region of birth or residence for older persons plus the sequential number coding the sexes, plus the check digit, that is the actual maticni broj, and most deficiencies are related to this component and, who knows, perhaps there will be 30 per cent deficient missing whatsoever. But for us, the date of birth is the crucial part of it, and this is reported quite well in the census. So the percentage of missing date of births would be approximately 2 per cent, something like that. So it is not 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: I'm telling you that the percentage of inaccuracies is 30 to 40 per cent. That is the position of the Defence, and we will elaborate it. Did you in your research deal with the causes of certain demographic occurrences in Bosnia and Herzegovina, causes and effects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, did deal with the effects. These are the demographic consequences. But I didn't discuss the causes as such.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Would you be able to give an estimate for this period you dealt with? There is a war period in that time-frame, and the time proceeding the electoral lists in 1997, 1998. Do you have compounded data for these two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean. I don't understand the question exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: It's a very clear question. Did you follow the trends in the distribution of population after the war, that is to say, between 1995 and 1998, and were there any changes that you would call dramatic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned earlier today, for the war period we lack sources of information about the population, and also for the years after the war, sources are extremely limited, and we don't have population record as such. So it is hard to say what was the population dynamics in the years until the 1997-8 election. But of course, some information exists and I looked at this information, and unfortunately these are mainly population projections. The most serious ones were made for the post-war period by the United Nations Social Economic Division in New York and they estimated the size of the population in this period. Some presented some trends in -- in the birth rates, mortality rates and migration. Another source that exists for these years is the UNHCR. This is United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and why this source is relevant? It's relevant because of the returns, of course, and in particular returns of the minority groups. As we all remember, in the Dayton Peace Agreement there is a whole chapter about the importance of people returning home. So conditions must -- had to be created to make it possible for people to return home. As I mentioned yesterday, we are speaking of more than 2 million people who at the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina were displaced, were not living at their place of residence, pre-war place of residence. And a majority group among these two -- more than 2 millions were minorities. So these are people who moved out from territories that are no more in hands of their ethnic group after the war. So minority returns is a very important issue. So I did study the minority returns for these years. And unfortunately for the years directly after the war, the minority returns are not very frequent. Why? Because there is no yet good political climate for this. The situation is still very sensitive. So people are waiting, waiting until the situation will improve, that they will be able to -- to go home. So I did study some sources, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: You speak about changes in terms of return. However, after the Dayton Peace Accords, 150.000 Serbs moved out of Sarajevo to the territory of Republika Srpska. Can that change be considered dramatic in the entire framework of internally displaced people after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am unaware of these 150.000 Serbs. There were, of course, Serbs who moved out of Sarajevo. And Sarajevo is just one of the examples of split municipalities, several Sarajevo municipalities were split, and one part of a municipality was decided to be a federation, another part Republika Srpska. It was quite a common phenomenon for the split municipalities that people moved within the municipalities. So the Serbs from the federal part went to the Serb part, and the Bosniaks and the other non-Serbs from the Serb part went to the federal part. So I'm sure there were Serbs who had to leave certain parts of Sarajevo and move to the RS territories. Of course whether it was dramatic, I think -- well, hard to tell without having an exact number. I think for many groups this movement, forced movement, were dramatic. For every person it was dramatic, I think. Every single person who was -- who had to move out and go to another place, it's a dramatic change in life, most definitely. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Change is also dramatic from the point of view of the number of those who left. But let me ask you this: In the Milosevic case, you also included 26 municipalities in the federation. Not the entire federation, just these municipalities. And if we compare data for the total population, the change in the national -- sorry, in the ethnic make-up of the population in the Republika Srpska and the part of the federation you studied is as follows in percentages according to you: In Republika Srpska, the change is minus 95 per cent of the Muslims; and in the federation, it goes up to minus 88 per cent of Serbs. Do you recall these percentages that you discussed in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I don't recall exact numbers, I am not surprised with what you are saying. This is what I said a few minutes ago. So that is the nature of what happened in the country like Bosnia and Herzegovina. The country has been split into two parts. One part is the RS, one is the federation. So people moved. The Serbs from the federal part went to the RS. The non-Serbs from RS, mainly Muslims, moved out and moved to -- into the federation. So that is what happened. The -- the -- you know, if you look at the change in the ethnic composition for the entire country, the changes are minor, I could -- I would say for the entire country. But if you go down and you look at the changes for the political entities, the changes will be dramatic, and for the RS they will be opposite to those that we will see in the federation. So that is the nature of these moments. That is what happened during this war. There were huge movements of the population, and the -- the Dayton line actually split the country along the ethnic lines. That is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I would like to suggest to you in order to allow Mr. Cvijetic to ask as many questions as possible within the time-frame to give short answers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: You have almost anticipated my next question. You would agree with me, I suppose, that Bosnia-Herzegovina has a certain body of population that we've just divided into ethnic groups, and the moving out of one ethnic community, or a certain part of that community, into another entity, for instance, the move of Muslims from Republika Srpska in the -- into the federation, would increase the percentage of Serbs in the total population of Republika Srpska and would also increase the percentage of Muslims in the total population of the federation. You will agree with me that this is the principle of connected vessels. If a certain population gets reduced in percentage in one entity, its percentage in the other entity will increase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, roughly speaking. There is also this newcomers component; right? So it depends who is moving in in addition to these people who move out. But in roughly speaking, it is a system like that.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: I think we agree on this line of questioning, because you seem to be anticipating all my questions. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is -- has a certain body of population. It does not have any reserve Muslims, reserve Serbs, and reserve Croats. So this principle of connected vessels functions. Would you get similar findings if you included in your sums the Serbs who moved from Croatia into Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were some Serbs, Croatian Serbs, who moved into Bosnia. That is correct. The number wasn't that high. As far as I remember, it was 25.000 of Croatian Serbs reported by the year 2000 in the governmental system of registration of internally displaced persons and refugees. So 25.000 of new-coming Serbs from Croatia compared to the overall population size of -- at the end of the war, as estimated by the UN, 3.5 million people, I think it is a very small number. I think it wouldn't have any significant impact on the ethnic composition unless they would, all the 25.000, moved into one municipality. I wouldn't see it as a significant contributing to the increased fractions of the Serb population in many -- in practically all municipalities of Republika Srpska after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: The system of samples that you used in the Milosevic case when you selected seven municipalities covers in terms of data around 212.000 Muslims. That is 12 per cent of the total number of Muslims in 109 municipalities. And there were about 1.905.000 of them. I would like to know if this sample could be sufficiently representative in these seven selected municipalities to provide general demographic conclusions for the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this sample concept here is completely unclear to me. It is seven municipalities, whole municipalities. On one hand we have for them the census data 1991 complete. On the other hand we have the voters records for matching, et cetera. So I think the seven municipalities are seven municipalities. That's all I can say. I presented separate statistics for seven municipalities, for 47 municipalities, and for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. So we don't need any samples for Bosnia. We have complete statistics for the entire country.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: You spoke about refugees. In fact, you determined their number based on the number of registered voters abroad, and that's what you called them, voters who registered to vote from abroad. That number also contains the number of citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina who had been there earlier, before the war, so-called economic emigres. You attached to all of them the status of refugees, and you calculated that including them in the statistics would bear a margin of error, margin of statistical error, of 4.6 per cent. Would you tell me, what is the -- the generally tolerable margin of error in statistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we usually speak when we think of inferential statistics that 5 per cent error is the tolerable error. Of course there might be a lower error, 1 per cent error, 3 per cent, 4 per cent. So these are the ranges of acceptable error.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Right. Then we see that this threshold is gone, and it's all used up on the margin of error created by including all the people abroad into the category of refugees. And if we add to that the error, the mathematical error of including Yugoslavs and the effect of ignoring the 150.000 Serbs who moved out of Sarajevo, the number of those who came from Croatia, the mistakes in ID numbers, the mistakes in bias inherent in the sources of data like the one I just pointed out, especially in terms of casualties and missing persons, and the errors in the calculation of the initial original number of persons who were of age at the critical moment, that is to say, those born before 1980, and I intend to show you a table about that if we have time, then the total sum of these errors multiplies your threshold, and we get a very significant percentage of error. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't think the witness should be required to answer that question. It's obviously the first plank in Mr. Cvijetic's closing remarks on -- on this area of this bit of evidence. But it isn't something that allows a question that the witness could answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if it is not, I agree with you. In any case, it will be relevant for our demographic expert who will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, do you agree with me that on the changes in ethnical structure, trends in distribution, and total population potentials of individual ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are over a longer historical period several -- or, rather, numerous socio -- socio and natural factors impacting? Would you agree with me? MR. DI FAZIO: I object, if Your Honours please. We're getting back into that area of factors in -- affecting population potentials of individual ethnic groups. I don't see how that's possibly relevant to the central questions of movement of people and numbers of deaths. You can see where this is going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Cvijetic has five minutes left. If he wishes to use it in this manner and if the witness can venture an opinion, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may answer, yes? In the population development there are always natural factors. That is birth, deaths. There is migration, and there are socio-economic factors. Of course we are speaking about prosperity and safety and the political climate. It all has an impact on how the population develops. But this is -- I think we are talking now -- at least I'm talking in my reports about a very special period. It is about the war period, and one has to agree that in the war period there are extraordinary factors operating that bring certain consequences, demographic consequences of war. And even though I didn't study causes of the demographic phenomena like migration and war-related deaths, it is of course true to -- to -- to say war was one of the crucial factors that caused these consequences, and that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: Is one of the results of demographic movements in Bosnia and Herzegovina something that led to ethnic territorial homogenisation, and is the ethnic map of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a result now simpler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by homogeneous here. Well, the homogeneous is the ethnic composition within every political entity. Meaning that Serbs are mainly living in the RS and Bosniaks and Croats in the federation, and they have -- and each group is dominant in almost every municipality in each political entity. But country-wide, I wouldn't call it a homogenisation of the country because that is the opposite of what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: I wasn't talking about the state. I was talking about ethnic territorial homogenisation. Are you aware that political factors affect this ethnic territorial homogenisation as well as economic factors, geographic factors, and sociopsychological factors? Are you aware of all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not my area, really. I didn't study that, and I would be, I think -- I -- I don't think I have an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: THE END OF THIS
utterances.text: In your opinion, was the decision of one part of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina to leave the country and go live elsewhere in Western Europe and even across the ocean affected by the liberalisation of immigrant visas for these countries and the opportunity to see their economic problems resolved in that way as well? MR. DI FAZIO: What period of time are we talking about, the 1970s when the guest workers left Yugoslavia? Are we talking about the period of time after Dayton? It seems -- the question's just lacking any clarity at all, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, it's 12.06. It's time for the adjournment, and that is the end of Mr. Cvijetic's cross-examination. Mr. Di Fazio, when we return, we will -- your very brief re-examination and then -- then the next witness, I suppose. MR. DI FAZIO: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I would indicate that we have confirmed the availability of this courtroom for an extended sitting tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one minute before you finish. This will take just one minute of your time. For me to complete the cross-examination of Mrs. Tabeau, I need one session, and I apply to you to grant me that session or to recall Mrs. Tabeau at a different time for me to conclude, because the time you granted me was certainly not sufficient, and it's certainly below the time allocated to us. In one more session, I have more questions for Mrs. Tabeau, and I also have practical examples to present that will illustrate the significance of all I've said so far. And if you have made a concession to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber has ruled on this question and I have no intention of re-opening it. Yes. We take the adjournment. Sorry, before we rise, I had in phrasing my question to Mr. Di Fazio referred to what I anticipated would be at best a very brief re-examination. Could you confirm that you have any questions in redirect, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Zero, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. In which case, we thank you, Ms. Tabeau, for your assistance, and you are now released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Is the Prosecution ready with its next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, perhaps before we proceed to that there's just one matter left over from the last witness. I understand that you want me to read formally into the record the reports and associated exhibits that the Prosecution seeks the admission of. Firstly 10397, 65 ter 10397. That's the IDP case report. The expert report prepared in the Milosevic case and that's 10398. The addendum report, that's 10399. Some corrected pages to the addendum report, that's 10399.1. The victims of war report, that's 10400. The corrigendum that was prepared before the summer break, that's 10400.01. And the summary of principal findings of the report -- the victims of war report, that's 10400.02, and they're all the -- that's the list there. And if Your Honours please, I will excuse myself now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Could you remind me as to whether we need to make a formal order for admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So ordered. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have the same objection -- before admitting this document, we wanted to repeat our objection given the specific position Ms. Tabeau occupies as an OTP employee. We do not believe the threshold is met for admitting this expert report as an independent report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the behalf of Mr. Stanisic's Defence, I propose that the report be rejected in its entirety, or that the Chamber assign a very low probative value to it in view of the very little time we were given in our attempt to prove that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We're aware of the position -- the general position of Defence counsel on this, and so noted. It's now on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, Your Honours, 65 ter 10397 will be Exhibit P01626. 65 ter 10398 will be Exhibit P01627. 65 ter 10399 will be Exhibit P01628. 65 ter 10399.1 will be P01629. 65 ter 10400 will be P01630. 65 ter 10400.01 will be P01631. And 65 ter 10400.02 will be P01632. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in can I very briefly revert to the question of the testimony of Ewan Brown, just to explain to Your Honours why Your Honours may have thought that we slightly cavalierly when Your Honours adjourned his cross-examination said in that case we wouldn't be calling him in October. There is a very good reason. Mr. Brown, as I think was explained to you, is now a self-employed contractor. He obtained a three-month job in a continent quite a long way away from here, which began, I believe, about a few weeks ago. As effectively a favour, he agreed that he would lose a week's work to come here to testify, and therefore a week's money, but, Your Honour, it seemed to us that if his cross-examination were to be adjourned, it would be unfair to ask someone who is now self-employed to give up that -- the earnings he could make for that week to travel a great deal of distance, which would also put the Tribunal to more expense, in order to testify for something like four hours and be sent away again, and so that's why we decided that it would be more sensible that his evidence be given as a whole, and we can fill the gap with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. Indeed the -- we were reminded of Mr. Hannis, I believe it was, who had in effect asked the Chamber to reconsider the oral ruling that was given, and having so reconsidered it, we are satisfied, especially because the -- the Defence inferentially supports this, that the more efficient use of time, apart from the personal circumstances of the witness to which you have just brought our attention, is such that the entirety of his testimony, that is, examination-in-chief and cross-examination, be postponed until January, and we are hoping that it's the first week in January, the week beginning the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, sorry my microphone's gone off. Your Honours, yes. I understand that's the first week back. And, Your Honours, at some stage could we perhaps return to the question of timetabling after the conclusion of the Prosecution case, because I know there's some doubt about whether we really will finish the rest of the evidence in November, but I think there's a high likelihood. So in the light of what was said in open court by His Honour Judge Delvoie about timetabling, I think it may be of assistance to all parties if at some stage we could return to what is actually going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In that vein, Ms. Korner, we trust that Mr. Hannis didn't overspeak when he said that the removal -- or that the deferring of Mr. Brown's testimony from October wouldn't -- wouldn't result in lost days. So there is another witness that you can slot in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, yes. We can certainly -- there will be no lost days there. What I'm actually -- sorry, what I'm talking about is the conclusion of all the Prosecution evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know. It's just that I thought I should also raise that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, we are certainly going to fill the gap, Your Honours. So having said that, there's nothing to stop the next witness coming in. Your Honours, may I say that there's no problem about his travel arrangements provided he had can finish tomorrow giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, a short preliminary issue regarding the witness, the next witness. As far as I could see from the list of documents that -- provided by the OTP, there are ten documents which are not on the 65 ter list, out of which, in turn, a number of them had not been disclosed to the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the witness needs to remain outside court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree. Sorry, Your Honour. I think it's -- can the witness be removed from the courtroom for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through our legal assistant we advised the OTP of those documents. We sent a list to them. Having in mind the change in schedule of the witness and the circumstances surrounding his testimony, we are against the Prosecution using them during their examination-in-chief, and we would oppose having those documents admitted since there was no formal request put in to add them onto the list, and they should not be used in redirect either so as not to have them admitted through the back door.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, actually, this seems to be turn and turnabout as to who's trying to raise more objections about this witness, but it was Ms. Savic who sent an e-mail complaining that some of the documents were not on our 65 ter list. I accept that. At the moment I have no intention of trying to move them into evidence. One of them is purely a memory-refreshing document. Others we'll see where we go, but at the moment I accept that they're not on our 65 ter. I do not propose to try to make them exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What about disclosure, Ms. Korner? There would be five documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These are all documents, Your Honour, that were shown to the witness in his interview with the OTP. For some unknown reason, formal disclosure does not seem to have taken place. I don't know why that is, but we accept that. However, I don't think the Defence can say they're prejudiced, because they got the list. The documents themselves are all contained in EDS. They're not documents that they couldn't -- the Defence couldn't see. They got the list two or three days ago. They're all short documents. If the Defence say in some way they're prejudiced, then perhaps they can explain how. But, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I don't know how it was, but it -- it somehow escaped our attention that documents that had actually been shown in interview had not formally been disclosed. Having said that, we've never had a request for the disclosure of these documents either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will see where we go. Could the -- there are no protective measures with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Sorry. Mr. Smith reminds me I should have said e-court. I said EDS. It should have been e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I trust you can hear me, sir. Would you be so kind as to make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The solemn declaration that you have just made exposes you to the penalties for perjury which this Tribunal is empowered to impose should you give false or misleading testimony. Would you begin by giving us your name, your date of birth, and your profession, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Slobodan Avlijas, and I was born on the 18th of April, 1945, in the village of Rudnik, Ilidza municipality, the city of Sarajevo. I hold a law degree, and I'm currently retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You say you're currently retired. Did you retire from practice as a lawyer or in some other field of work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never acted as attorney. I worked as part of the judiciary. For the last two years of my career I worked in the security centre on a range of issues such as being a member of the commission tasked with searching for the missing persons on behalf of Republika Srpska. I was appointed to that position in 1995. Before that, I worked on education and transitional courses given to employees of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. I also held a number of other positions within the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you testified previously either before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in one of the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. I testified before the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Momcilo Mandic case, as well as Lalovic and Skiljevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In this case you have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, and the procedure which is fairly common among courts is that you -- the side calling you would begin, after which the side opposite would have an opportunity to ask you questions arising out of your testimony, and then the Prosecution would have an opportunity for re-examination arising out of the cross-examination. At that point, or indeed at any earlier point, the Bench itself may have questions of you. The Prosecution has indicated that their examination-in-chief should last for three hours, and counsel for each of the accused have -- counsel for the first accused has indicated three hours and counsel for the second accused two hours. So that's a total of eight -- eight hours that is expected that your testimony would take. The Court, of course, does not sit continuously, and indeed the sessions do not exceed an hour ninety minutes for technical reasons having to do with the tapes that have to be changed, the tapes that record the proceedings of the Tribunal, and that also allows for the comfort of -- of the witness, counsel, and indeed everybody involved. But notwithstanding those set breaks, if there are any points at which you yourself would need to take a break, if you indicate that we would accommodate you. You are beginning your testimony in the third session of the ordinary sittings of the court, and we will rise at 1.45, but we will return at 2.30 and rise for the day at 4.00 and resume your testimony tomorrow morning at 9.00. And with that, I would invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, can we begin briefly by just going through the steps by which you come to testify today. I think it's right that you were originally interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 11th of December of 1997, and that was almost entirely about the inspection you made of the camps, detention facilities, in October 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct. However, I wouldn't call it an inspection. We simply visited those locations. Had it been an inspection, it would have had the prerogative of supervision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Visits. And you actually provided copies to the Office of the Prosecutor on that occasion of some of the documents that you yourself had. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you were interviewed again by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 13th of August of 2006. It was a tape-recorded interview, and you were interviewed as a potential witness and not as a suspect. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As you've already told the Court, you testified on behalf of Momcilo Mandic at the trial in the Bosnian court, and that testimony was in 2007. And then did you also testify in December 2009, on behalf of Mr. Lalovic and the gentleman with the first name of Soniboj at their trial at the state court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think, as we know, Mr. Mandic was acquitted, this was the crimes trial, and Mr. Lalovic and the other gentleman were convicted. And I think before actually you testified in the Lalovic trial you'd also been interviewed by the prosecutor in that particular case. I should say the prosecutor in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Everything you enumerated is correct. With one remark, though. Lalovic and Skiljevic did not receive their final judgements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the sense that the conviction is subject to appeal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, I think you saw both Defence counsel in this case, Mr. Krgovic, and Mr. Cvijetic, on Monday and Tuesday of this week. Is it right that you now live in the Bijeljina -- the town of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And for how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Since January 1, 1993, when I had my Ministry of Justice office moved to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, can I ask you this: Did you watch any of the other witnesses, in particular Mr. Mandic, who have given evidence in this case? Did you watch the testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I did not follow this case at all, but I did follow Mr. Mandic's testimony in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All right. Can I now very briefly also, because I know that you're anxious to get away, just deal with your professional background which you've described to the Office of the Prosecutor in your interview. I think it's right that you started work -- well, you didn't start work, but in August of 1974, were you appointed as the secretary of the District Prison in Sarajevo where you remained until September 1978, and then became the president of the Municipal Court in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: For misdemeanors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For misdemeanors. After that, which lasted until 1986, you had two mandates, were you appointed as deputy of the inter-municipality district attorney, and did you remain in that position until 1992 officially?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I have a correction to make. I was appointed -- well, probably in the Western world it is an unknown instance. That is the assistant inter-municipality ombudsman for self-governance. We were tasked with protecting the rights of workers and state-owned property in the ten municipalities which did not make part of metropolitan Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's come directly, please, to the outbreak of the conflict in April of 1992. At that stage were you actually working?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: At the time in 1992, the Law on Companies was passed, declaring null and void the Law on Associated Labour which had dealt with the issues I worked on as assistant ombudsman for self-management. I remained as the sole person in the office, whereas the others left looking for work. I was effectively out of work, and as such, I saw the breakout of the conflict. In other words, that particular state body was to be abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time in May that you by chance met Mr. Lalovic together with Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, I was returning from Pale, using a roundabout road via Tvrdemici, and I passed by the building of the correctional penal facility Kula, and I saw the vehicle of my former colleague, Laloj Radovic [as interpreted], nicknamed Ratko, and out of pure curiosity I went in to ask him if he was going home. I found him together with Mr. Mandic, and I heard that Mr. Mandic was named minister of justice to a Ministry of Justice that was to be established and that I was going to be appointed to work there, too, which was very good news, because I was trying to avoid being mobilised and I was more or less in hiding in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who told you that you were going to be appointed to the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: There's something wrong with the question. Nobody every told me that I was going to be minister, and I didn't hear that. I heard that he was invited to participate in the organisation of the new Ministry of Justice. Apart from Momcilo Mandic, there was nobody else appointed by the Presidency. He was appointed minister of justice, and he found Ratko Lalovic in his weekend cottage. They went down to Kula together, and that was a mission to find new staff, to go head-hunting for the future staff of the regular courts, et cetera. So there was no talk about a specific job, just involvement in the establishment of the justice system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there must have been a mishearing by somebody because I didn't ask whether you were going to be appointed the minister but to the ministry. But in any event, who was telling you that they wanted you in the ministry? Can I emphasise that. Was that Mr. Mandic or Mr. Lalovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I found them together sitting in an office, and Ratko said to Momcilo, "Here comes a man who can help us if he joins us to do this work," and then both of us asked in unison, "Right. Who do you know? Who else can we recruit?" That's how the conversation went. And I think I went to Ilidza from there, and I joined in this effort only in end May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Okay. Can I just urge you, Mr. Avlijas, to answer my questions as shortly as possible. As I said -- as I say, if I want more information, I'll ask you for it. Now, we will see in various --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll see in some of the documents that you're referred to or addressed as during 1992 the deputy minister of justice. Did you ever receive in 1992 a formal appointment as deputy minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. At the outset, it was Nenad Radovic who was appointed deputy minister of justice. He was the only deputy to be elected after Momcilo Mandic. But you can see from the documents that I was first named assistant minister in early November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just let's see if we can get a date by which you were working. You had an opportunity, I think, to read through the bundle of documents that the Prosecution have, and one of them was an intercept between -- an intercepted conversation between Mr. Kovac and Mr. Mandic on the 26th of May. Now, I'm not interested in the contents of that except for this: There's a reference to you, I think you heard or saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to bother putting it up on the screen. One, it's not on our 65 ter, and the only interest is for the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mandic says to Kovac - and for the Defence this is on the second page of the intercept - that you are already working with him. So and that's the 26th of May. So does that date accord with your recollection of when you started work with Mr. Mandic or with the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: If I remember well, that intercept was in July, and I got to Kula in end May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I don't think it matters too much. By the end of May you were already working.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That's right. I think it was the 26th or the 28th of May, my first day at work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you got to Kula at the end of May. Now, why did you go to Kula? I'm sorry, first of all, I'll run that back. What was Kula at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Kula was an abandoned correctional penal facility of the open type, which at the beginning of the war was occupied by the Territorial Defence unit of the Kasindol Battalion. I don't know what it was called at that time, but when we got there, I know there was a police station inside. There was some military units inside. There were tanks around the compound. In one of the buildings there were even refugees housed. That's how we found it. When we got there, we didn't even have offices to work in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say there was a police station inside. Which police station was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't know how it was organised. I'm afraid to make a mistake if I tell anything specific. I think it was part of the Novi Grad police station or perhaps the Ilidza police station. I -- I know there was a police station, and I know who the chief was. Do you -- do you need to know the names of the senior staff? Their office was in the former KP Dom administration, and the name was Radenko Vujicic. At the to the compound of the KP Dom there was a policeman standing and checking the comings and goings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So -- that's the next question I was going to ask you. The police were actually in charge of the security at that stage, were they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. They were there for security, because you could not enter the compound before showing authorisation to the policemen at the gate, and there were police officers inside too. They were probably guarding whatever needed to be guarded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look, please, now, briefly at a document which is 1D00-164. And that's tab 2.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Where am I supposed to see that? Oh, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it will come up on the screen. Now this, decision --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the second page in both the English and B/C/S. Can we go to the second page in B/C/S possibly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- was passed apparently on the 1st of May by the Presidency. So before you started your job, but I think it's right that you're familiar with this decision. Is that correct, Mr. Avlijas?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was part of my job later to -- to be familiar with this regulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's -- if we go back, please, to the first page in each, English and B/C/S. The decision was that on the establishment of the penitentiary re-education institutes in the territory of the Serbian Republic, and it effectively deals with, as it says, the establishment of these institutions. And it says under Article 5, the current staff of the penitentiary and re-educational organisation will continue to be in charge of security with the assistance of the Ministry of the Interior police forces. Well, the ministry -- the MUP as needed. Now, was that something that had been happening before the conflict in April, or was that something new, that the police should assist in -- with security?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It was nothing new. As a general rule, sentence was supposed to be enforced in keeping with the Law on Enforcement of Sentences that was taken over from the previous law unless -- unless clashing with the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That means that the police would be active in preventing riots, organised escapes. And in view of the specific wartime circumstances, police assistance would be asked if there occurred an external attack. But from 1992 to 1997, during my tenure, police officers were never involved in the execution and the enforcement of penalties and sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you were sent to Kula, and what was the reason that you were sent to Kula?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What was the reason they sent me to Kula?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, Kula was the seat of the Ministry of Justice. Mr. Mandic came down from Pale and said that part of the offices of the Ministry of Justice would be here on the premises of the penal correctional facility. Later on, they moved us to different premises on Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: And Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes. And Bijeljina. Were there any prisoners at Kula when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We discussed yesterday the terms "detainee," and "prisoners." There were very few, in fact just one detainee who was guilty of a traffic violation and had nowhere else to go, but as for prisoners whom we found in the part of the correctional facility where sentences were served, we saw several prisoners. We were able to see them only in the mornings when we had breakfast in the refectory, and then it was their turn to have breakfast, but they were in the part of the facility to which we had no access.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, can you just explain to us what in your understanding is the difference between a detainee and a prisoner, briefly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: A detainee is -- sorry, a prisoner is a person taken prisoner during combat and brought onto certain premises. They have nothing to do with the Ministry of Justice. An inmate is a person who was sentenced by a regular court. And a person in custody is a person who was remanded in custody by decision of the competent court, awaiting trial. Those are the three categories. The latter two categories are the exclusive -- fall within the exclusive purview of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So just so that we all understand that, a prisoner, somebody taken during combat, in other words, a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is defined also by the International Law of Warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And to which the Geneva Conventions apply?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you have an inmate, as you call it, a person who has been sentenced by a court and is serving that sentence, and finally, someone who is being investigated, if you like, remanded -- that has been remanded in custody before a trial.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so in Kula, when you got there, you -- you said to us a moment ago -- sorry. There was somebody serving a sentence for the traffic violation, and then the prisoners that you could only see in the mornings, who were they? Do you mean prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: First of all, that one person had nowhere to go, and he remained to work in our workshop. He was named Slavko, and he worked as a mechanic. He was no longer treated as a detainee. And these other people, they were not convicts. They were prisoners. They were not people who were convicted. They were taken prisoner, I suppose, in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever make any inquiries as to what these people were doing there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, we asked out of normal human curiosity who are these people, and we were told they were prisoners. Nobody has access to them except their guards. We could see them only from a distance. We could see them in the morning when they were going to have breakfast.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a small objection to the transcript. This is not in the indictment, and I don't see any reason to deal in such great detail with a facility that is not included in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to come on to -- it's what happened to these people afterwards that's the relevant -- and indeed the categorisations that the witness has just been talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to have a look now, please, at the document which is number 3 in the binder, 0 -- 65 ter 01434.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know what the scrawl on the -- that's being shown on the screen. Could we have the front of not whatever that scrawl is for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Page 1. Sorry. Thanks. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is The Book of Duty Transfer for the KP facility at Kula, and I think you've had a chance to go through that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that shows -- I think you are able to comment on a number of the actual matters, but was this the book that was kept by the police at the time between, if we go to the next page, the 1st of May --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next page in English, please. And it's the third page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it records who was bought -- brought to the prison. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, I think we need for the entry I want -- can we go to the next page in B/C/S, 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This says there, taking this first entry, that on the 2nd of May, 1992, criminal inspectors Vaskovic and Tusevljak took from the SM in Kula to Pale the following persons, and it lists those persons. Do you know on what authority the apparently police inspectors were taking people from Kula to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question because I didn't work in internal affairs. I don't know why these people were taken to Kula. I can only suppose it was for interrogation. But you can see from this log that it is a log of transition of duty, a log of rotations in Kula, and you can see the status of the police in Kula. This log-book was kept by their supervisor, Soniboj Skiljevic, and we found it when they were leaving Kula in the end of July 1992 and we kept it in our archives. In fact, the warden kept it in his archives, and it was found later during a search conducted by SFOR, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come back to how you knew all about it, but what I'm just trying to get at the moment on this one entry is if these people are in custody within a prison, who has to give the authority to have people taken out of a prison? Who has to give the -- the order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: If we look at the decree and the instruction on the treatment of inmates, you can see that the corps command bears most of the responsibility. They have the greatest authorisations in the hierarchy for prisoners. From our practice, I know that nobody -- no prisoner could get out of Kula without a warrant from the military security. They had to give their approval for exchanges, for taking prisoners out for labour duty and any other thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're assuming, are you, that these people were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I suppose so, because they were not in custody, and they were not treated as convicts. They can only be prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's just have a look at one other entry, please, for the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is on page 3 in the English, and it's on page 4 in the B/C/S, I think. Five, sorry. Five. That's fine, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 3rd of May, and I appreciate all of this was before you got there, the following persons were arrested by the MUP in Ilidza, and it names all these people. In order for the police to place somebody in custody as these people apparently were because they're brought into the prison, did there have to be an order from the judge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: You know, this was at a time of imminent threat of war. The state of war had not yet been proclaimed. Now, employees in the police, according to the Law on National Defence, if so required by the army or the circumstances, were supposed to be a component in combat units with the proviso that they would be subordinated to the Supreme Command. Now, whether these people who were brought into the facility had been captured in combat, in which case they would have been prisoners of war, or they had been brought in without any warrant, perhaps, yes, the police were able to hold people in custody for 45 or 72 hours, I don't remember, if they were caught in the act, or perhaps these people were members of a combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this finally on this document, or two questions: Did you ever find any records when you took over the running of the prisoners, you've told us, at the end of July, explaining why these people were there, under what authority they were being kept there, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, you see, when we took over the correctional penal facility in end July, we found prisoners from the Hadzici municipality. They were captured by military units in Hadzici, and they were kept in the sports hall for a whole month before being transferred to the barracks in Lukavica, and they were held for a while in the barracks where there was no room for them anymore. There had been 200 people there already. And on the order of the corps commander, as I later found out, they were transferred to the correctional penal facility Kula, and the employees of Kula were ordered to guard them and to feed them on the premises. The rest of the supervision was in the hands of military security and the army. Every time they were removed from the facility it had to be approved by the military security and the army, equally their approval was required for taking them out for any reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand if the army sends people in that's one thing, but what I'm talking about is where the police apparently brought these people in that we saw the list of, did you find any records of whether there'd been an order by the judge or what had happened to these people or who these people were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We found no records whatsoever when they left the facility. They took all their documentation with them save for this single notebook which was either discarded or forgotten. This is the extent of what my colleagues found.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So this book was the only record they left and which you found when you took over the facility at the end of the July. That's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: This book was found in a dustbin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I want to ask any more questions on that. Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01633, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after Kula, were -- sorry. Just for a moment. Did you actually take part in -- during the course of June in the organisation and establishment of Municipal Courts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Municipal misdemeanour courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Municipal misdemeanour courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at the document which -- well, we can't maybe. Your Honours, I've made a note, but I see it's one that wasn't on our 65 ter list. So I just need to check to see whether I actually need to ask the witness to have a look at it. Well, Your Honours, I do. I simply want the witness to refresh his memory about this, but before I do so I'll ask if there's an objection. It's the document at tab 7, 10534, where there's a reference to what the witness did, and that's all I want to ask him to do, but I'll wait to hear if there's an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there an objection to show him the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection. We agree to it being used to refresh the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, could we have up, please, document 10534.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the date must be an error, because we'll see a reference to --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I made that note when I revisited the documents. It should be the 4th of July, 1992. We can see from it that the visit to Trebinje was on the 23rd, 25th, and 25th [as interpreted] of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we just -- that's exactly what I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go over to, please, the next page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, who signed that report? Before we did that, before we move on, whose signature is that? Is that Mr. Mandic's?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't know if it's Mandic's or Nenad Radovic's. I do think that Momcilo had a different signature. But it -- it could be Radovic's signature. If I were to see Mr. Mandic's original signature, I'd be able to compare. In -- in the other case, it would be Mr. Radovic's, who was assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry. I don't think it's important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just go, please, then, quickly to the next page. We see there that the Justice Ministry work group comprising --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I remind you of the procedure to allow the witness to read the document and then formulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just have a quick look at that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: You can go ahead with the question. I know this document by heart.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Right. First of all, I want to ask you, it says -- is what it says correct, namely, that it was you, Mr. Branko Mandic [indiscernible], and Mr. Velasevic who visited the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The team consisted of Predrag Nikolic, Slobodan Avlijas, Branka Mandic and not Branko, and Igor Velasevic. Predrag Nikolic and Slobodan Avlijas visited Herzegovina and Trebinje, whereas the other two went down to Foca. They created that part of the report. Mr. Nikolic, who was in charge of organising the work of regular courts and prosecutors' offices had his part to do in Trebinje, and I accompanied him because I was in charge of correctional facilities. I think there is a separate report drafted by Mrs. Mandic and Mr. Velasevic regarding Trebinje and Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First thing that I want to ask you about this: Was a court actually established in Trebinje at this time, namely, June, July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, it was the time when personnel was chosen. That is why Predrag Nikolic was tasked with -- well, I think the decision on the election of judges had been issued by that time, and it was Nikolic's remit to implement it. I went to organise the work of misdemeanour courts which could begin operating in that part of Herzegovina since there were no more obstacles to take place. I simply went there to talk with the judges to see what problems they had. The point was to have a District Prison established in that area, because it was standard practice to have the seat of the District Prison in the same town where the District Court was, and it was for that reason that we wanted to establish the misdemeanour courts in other towns we visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you manage -- that was the next question. Did you manage to establish a district prison in that town at that stage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The District Prison in Trebinje is something that I fought for throughout that period. I wanted to have it established. But only as late as 1994 and 1995 we found an adequate location which was an abandoned dorm that could be transformed. Together with a construction company from Trebinje, we managed to restructure it. However, due to local authorities' obstructions, we never managed to have it up and running. It only started work -- its work in 1996. And before 1995, refugees were placed in that facility by Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter heard the last name correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be useful to have it clarified who Mr. Vucurevic was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the speaker of the Municipal Assembly in Trebinje and nothing could be done without him in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to direct the witness not to answer my interventions but to wait for the Prosecutor's question, and I apologise to Madam Korner. The witness was impatient.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Last question on Trebinje and this document. Was there any prison in Trebinje during 1992 which was actually under the control of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And finally on the document, Mr. Velasevic who's referred to there, can you tell us briefly, please, who was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Igor Velasevic was a lawyer who received his degree a year or two before the war. He was the son of my late friend Slobodan Velasevic, who was the centre Municipal Court president in Sarajevo. He introduced him to the judiciary, but he didn't remain within the judiciary for a long time. A couple of years later he went on to Switzerland and Canada. He did not hold any important positions. He was simply sheltered from the war in that way. For a while, his father was assistant minister for the judiciary. Later on he was transferred to Trebinje and then on to Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. It's my fault. It was a bad question. I meant what was his role in the Ministry of Justice at this stage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I couldn't define it. He was an employee of the Ministry of Justice. Something like an administrative inspector of sorts. I'm not really sure what he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he had worked with Mr. Mandic when Mr. Mandic was still part of the old Bosnian MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I cannot answer that with any certainty. I can only assume that he did, although I'm not sure. I really cannot say anything decidedly. I do know, however, that he was brought in the Ministry of Justice by Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would seem an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We are about to take the break. We will resume in -- in 45 minutes for our extended sitting. And the Chamber notes the co-operation, notes with appreciation the co-operation of the accused, who have been inconvenienced by this extended sitting. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, I inadvertently missed out a document that I wanted to ask you about in respect of still your time at Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen, please, document P1318.40, which is at tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a letter written to the -- in fact, the Ministry of Internal Affairs from, if we go to the second page, we can see it's the chief of SJB Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Second page in English, sorry. It's all one page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you said, you thought it was Novi Grad police station who was -- that were in Kula. And if we go back to the first page. The second -- the first paragraph relates to problems at Kula of reception, accommodation, food, hygiene, et cetera. And then it says: "After coordinating with the minister of justice and SJB under-secretary, on the 20th of May ... 114 persons were moved to the Vrbanja bridge area and sent into the city down Sokolovic Street. This group consisted of persons whose place of residence was in Gornji Kotorac in Dobrinja. "As they had been detained since the 12th of May ... the bureau for exchange in Ilidza was informed on two occasions but did not respond in time for possible exchange," and due to the objective problems, it was decided that this group be sent to the aforementioned locality. Now, just so that we understand, the Vrbanja bridge area and Sokolovic Street, are these just areas in the area of Greater Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The bridge Vrbanja is in the immediate vicinity of the government building. It is between the settlements of Grbavica and Skenderija. As for Mico Sokolovic Street, well, that's also downtown. Vrbanja was where the separation line was between the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time and the federation or what was then the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Do we understand from this letter that effectively these people were just kicked out of the prison?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure they were kicked out. There must have been an assessment to the effect that they no longer needed to be kept in custody. Throughout the war, all exchanges took place along separation lines, and the bridge on Vrbanja was a central location where forces, people moved from Republika Srpska into the federation and back. This is where civilians were usually released and exchanged. I am not familiar with this letter, though, and I wasn't privy to these issues at the time. I don't know why they were released. I suppose an agreement had been reached between the sides for their release.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under the law, can I just ask you this, Mr. Avlijas, was there any power to detain civilians, in other words, people who were not prisoners of war or who had been placed in custody by order of a court, because they had committed an offence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I can't say anything that would go beyond standard norms. A civilian cannot be a POW unless captured during combat. Logic dictates what a prisoner is under the laws of war. As for whether these were civilians or not, that is something I don't know. If they were civilians, we need first ascertain who had brought them to Kula in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You see, because you said a minute ago, "Throughout the war all exchanges took place along separation lines. The bridge on Vrbanja was a central location where forces -- people moved from Republika Srpska into the federation and back. This is where civilians were usually released and exchanged." Was that something that happened on a regular basis, that civilians were kept in custody in order to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I cannot decidedly say, but as far as I remember, in 1992 there was a massive occurrence following some arrangements that, say, a group of Serbs would go one way and another group the other way. There must have been arrangements in place, and that is why Vrbanja was a point of interest, irrespective of this case even. I just know it happened, but I don't know who organised such events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, sir. All I was asking was whether, because you said civilians were usually released and exchanged, was it standard practice, whether right or wrong, for civilians to be kept in custody to be used for exchange?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Now I understand. Vrbanja was a location where exchanges took place of POWs, dead bodies. So the Vrbanja bridge and the Bratstva and Jedinstva bridge. As for the group we are discussing now, that is to say, the inhabitants of Donji and Gornji Kotorac who had been detained in Kula, I don't know what their status was, whether they were POWs or not. As far as I remember, there had been military activities in 1992. Whether they were captured as civilians, that is something I don't know. In any case, they were probably released as civilians. I'm trying to think logically. Had there been POWs, they would not have been released without any POWs being offered in exchange. That is my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On that topic, could you have a look now, please, at a document which is P427.7, tab 8. Now, this is the -- dated the 6th of June. The central commission of the Serbian Republic for exchange of prisoners of war, detainees and bodies of the killed that are on the territory of the opposite side. Now, I don't know whether you saw this exact version of the document, but did you see some kind of version at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time when it was shown to me by the investigator named Nasir, I think it was, in 1998 -- sorry, 2008, 2009, after the trial of Momcilo Mandic. I had my first contact with Investigator Nasir and he showed me this order signed, I think, by Mr. Rajko Colovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, because you've got the dates slightly wrong, sir, but I'm not surprised because you've had quite a number of interviews, that your interview with Mr. Nasir was in -- remind myself, 2006, but --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you say that you saw it for the first time you told him that. Had you seen something like -- that's why I asked you the question the way I did, that you'd seen something like that published in the "Official Gazette"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't say that. All right. It doesn't -- I don't think I really mind, but could you have a look -- could we have a look, please, at page 3 in English and 2 in B/C/S. Do you see the paragraph that begins: "All women whose detention or deprivation of liberty is not related to the war or war activities, all children, all minors up to 16 years of age, old and helpless persons shall be released immediately ..." Does that document, in your view, support what you've just been saying, about there was no authority to lock up civilians and, in particular, it appears women, and children, minors, and the old?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, in fact, if you -- at the bottom of the page, and we need to go to the next page in English, a copy of that document went to the -- the Ministry of Justice, do we see? And everybody -- all police stations. But you never -- you never saw a copy of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, next can we look at some of the detention facilities that you were sent to inspect. First of all, did --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you sent to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, mid-June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who told you to -- to go there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Minister Mandic ordered Milenko Bileca, president of the court; Milorad Panjevic, the prosecutor; and me to go and gave us specific assignments, what we were supposed to do in Vogosca and Ilijas. Now, who gave an order to Momcilo Mandic, I don't know. It must have been someone from the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the specific assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The specific assignment was that all those in the field should be informed of the order of President Karadzic on the treatment of captured persons, because all sorts of stories were making the rounds in the media at the time. And my job was to hold talks with these two municipalities about establishing a misdemeanours court and to find an appropriate facility since a court had been set up already in Ilidza. A facility had to be found for enforcement of sentences. And of course we were to inspect the situation of those people who were captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what were the stories that were making the rounds?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, the media in Republika Srpska were blocked. You could hear news from Sarajevo that there were killings in Sarajevo on a daily basis, that the river was carrying bodies, all sorts of stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you said that it was -- the specific assignment was that those in the field should be informed of the order of President Karadzic on the treatment of captured persons. So what sort of stories were circulating about the treatment of captured persons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, bad stories. That's why we had to go out into this field mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm to going to ask you to be a little bit more specific. What do you mean by "bad stories"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That a large number of people were captured, that there were no conditions to hold them, that there were mass liquidations. That's what you could hear on Radio Sarajevo and read in the newspapers. Very ugly things, completely contrary to the Law on Warfare and the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so when Mr. Mandic told you to go to Vogosca, he specifically referred to these stories, did he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We all knew about that. We all listened to the radio and read newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you got to Vogosca, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We had a meeting in the Sonja facility with the leaders of the Crisis Staff of Vogosca, and there was also Professor Nikola Poplasen, who was a commissioner appointed by the government, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At that meeting was there anybody present from the SJB in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: If I can remember well, I think there was a blonde young man, Blagovcanin, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As well as having the meeting in the Sonja, did you go to the SJB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you meet anybody from the SJB called Brano Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Brano Vlaco was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And what did you understand his position was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: You could see by the way he acted that he was in charge of that camp in the immediate vicinity of the Sonja building, because when we discussed that problem, he was the one who spoke.
