He was in charge of security there, in charge of the guards for the captives, and that camp was right next to the building where we were holding the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Before we get on to that, what I'm trying to understand is he was in charge of that. Did you understand what position he held within the SJB at -- sorry, Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't know what his precise position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, but this was a leading question. The witness never said this person was part of the SJB. I think he first needs to be asked whether that person was with the SJB, if the witness knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question I asked him, because I didn't understand there was any dispute about this, is did you meet anybody from the SJB named Brano Vlaco, and he said Brano Vlaco was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, you understood him to be in charge of this camp, in charge of security. What did you understand, how did he come to be in charge of security?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was probably up to the Crisis Staff to decide. Somebody must have appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. That's fine. What did you understand was his job apart from being in charge of this camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go really into what his job was. We were more interested in doing our job and issuing the orders that followed from the order we received concerning the treatment of prisoners, depending on the situation as we found it on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Because our instructions related to all those present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. When you first met him at the Crisis Staff meeting that you attended in the restaurant Sonja or at the meeting you attended at the -- the restaurant Sonja, how was he introduced to you? In other words, how was it explained what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, he did the introduction himself. He said, "I'm chief of security for captured persons," because we were all supposed to say why we came to that meeting, and he did the same. That's what he said about himself. I saw him then for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Was he in uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In uniform. Which uniform I really can't remember after all this time, whether it was a police uniform or a military one. Especially because at that time everyone was wearing camouflage, civilians, army personnel, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we may come back to that. So there you are at this meeting, and you say there was this camp next door to Sonja's restaurant. Now, can you describe this camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It used to be a German bunker that was later adapted. Originally it was built to protect the railway. It was a concrete bunker whose exclusive purpose was to defend the railway. I don't know if it had an opening towards the sky. I don't know what it was like inside, but absolutely nonexistent conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you come to go there? Did you ask to see it or were you taken to see it or what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Nobody took us there. We held that meeting in the Sonja building, on the bank, and the bunker was only 50 metres away. So we could just see across that distance what it was like. Of course, we didn't go there, and if we had tried, nobody would have let us in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to ask you a little more about that. You've described it had nonexistent conditions. How do you know it had nonexistent conditions, and how do you know, if you didn't go and look at it, that it was a camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I was born in -- in the suburbs of Sarajevo, and there were seven or eight bunkers in the vicinity. There was one in Blazoj, where we played as children, climbed on top of it, and they are very familiar. I know what kind of structure that is, and I know that it's not a residential structure, so it's an inference I make.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, but -- but -- I'm so sorry. How do you know that the bunker was being used to hold people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: You could see people walking around the bunker, coming out, and they told us they were living in the bunker, and we could see for ourselves people coming and going. It's the same distance as from my seat to that door.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. How do you know that it was being held as a -- that people were being held in it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, they told us. They told us as soon as we came. We asked, "Where are these prisoners? Such and such stories are circulating." And they said, "There they in the bunker." Because when we came to give them instructions, we asked them, "Do you have prisoners of war?" "Where are they?" "There and there."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you go and look at them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We didn't go in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, did you go look -- did the bunker have a roof on it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It's a flat slab. I don't know if it had an opening looking at the sky. I'm not sure. I think it had. Now, according to the design, if I remember well these bunkers from my youth that I saw, I think there was an opening in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you say anything about that bunker to anybody who was present at that meeting at Sonja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Of course. The president of the court and I reacted the same. "Are you insane? Why are you keeping people there? The war won't last forever. Somebody will have to answer for this. There are Geneva Conventions and other conventions that have to be observed." We told them it was completely inappropriate and unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the reaction when you said this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, they said, "We'll have to sort this problem out," and in the meantime I looked for a different facility that could serve as a prison. They showed me a building, two or three storeys high, and then I ask the president of the court, since he chaired the meeting, whether there was any problem to transfer the prisoners there, and -- and the president of the court and I said, "You have to deal with it. You are keeping these people there. You make this decision, and now you want us to sort it out for you."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did anybody threaten you whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, this man came by -- at that time everybody was wearing rank insignia. I thought at first he was a colonel or something. And Bjelica and I both reacted rather explosively to the fact that these people were kept there. And then this man said, "If you are so sorry for them, would you like to join them?" I thought at first he was an officer, and then I later found out he was a village scoundrel who just pinned those rank insignia on him. He had been in prison before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us your job was to inspect these places because there were all these ugly rumours floating around about the treatment of prisoners. Given that you had been told that people were being held in a bunker, which you said was completely inappropriate, why didn't you go and have a look at the prisoners and fulfil your -- your duty there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I didn't dare. I didn't dare, especially when this guy came looking like an officer. How could I know who was in charge of what, who was doing what? We were newcomers there, and then only during the meeting we found certain things out. This came as a reaction before the official meeting even started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask what sort of people were being held there, whether they were civilians or people who were properly being captured in combat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We were told those were prisoners of war captured in battles in Vogosca, Svrake, Semizovac and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you help us, please, with a couple of photographs just to make sure we're all talking about the same place. Could you have a look, please, at 03 -- 03419.69, which is at tab 38.1. Now, are you able to tell us, looking at this aerial photograph, whereabouts the bunker was and Sonja's restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: This is the fork --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll give you a pen. Sorry, Mr. Avlijas. We'll give you a pen so you can mark the screen.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: This is the exchange connecting the road from Rajlovac. It goes towards Semizovac. And there is a connection to Vogosca. Sonja would be here in the vicinity, and the bunker close by.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Can you mark -- could you just -- I tell you what, put 1 for where the bunker is -- was -- is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Here, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we just --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: If I got it right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Are you marking Sonja's restaurant or the bunker?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Restaurant Sonja is here, marked, and the bunker is here below.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can that be marked -- admitted and marked as exhibit -- as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment. Perhaps it would be good to erase this and give the witness a chance to make a better marking and to put numbers 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just put the number 1, please, for where Sonja's restaurant is or was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And the bunker --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't see it, but it should be here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, and that may -- may that be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, quickly -- oh, P, sorry, yes. No. The Registrar's moved down the road.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1634, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could you now have, very quickly, a look at one -- a photograph that's already been exhibited, P1510. Tab 38.2. This photograph was taken quite recently, Mr. Avlijas, but is that the bunker that you're talking about? With a roof on, which it didn't have at the time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. No, that's not what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's good. All right. I appreciate -- the structure you saw didn't have a roof on, did it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Without the roof, would that be the structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: If you took the roof off, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I don't think I can proceed with this any further. Now, you say that on this visit you went to Vogosca and then to Ilijas. Where did you go in -- oh, I'm sorry, no. Before we leave Vogosca, you say you talked about -- you were shown a house where prisoners could be moved to. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Correct. In a settlement called Svrake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you remember what the house was called or did you subsequently discover what was house was called?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I learned later it was called Planeja's house.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Planjo's house, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Planjo's house. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you went to Planjo's house, who took you there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Some people from Vogosca. Brano Vlaco, perhaps, was with them. In any case, there were two or three local men who knew the place well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you -- did you ask how many people were in custody who were going to be moved, how many people were being kept in the bunker who were going to be moved to Planjo's house?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I asked or not. Perhaps I did; perhaps not. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, without knowing how many people were being kept, detained, how were you to know whether Planjo's house was suitable?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: When I saw that they were keeping people in a bunker that's two or three times smaller than Planjo's house, which was two-, three-storeys house, I thought Planjo's house must be adequate. This place was rather remote, not really prone to shelling. It satisfied other requirements. I was more interested in a facility appropriate for enforcing sentences, sentences meted out by basic court 2 in Ilidza, and covered Ilidza Vogosca, Hadzici, and Ilijas. That was our basic requirement for finding a proper facility, and then they had to scout for a building and that was their part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've already explained to us that there were only really three categories of prisoner, but did you make any attempt to find out who had ordered the detention of these people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did. I knew that in Vogosca the Crisis Staff operated just like in all other municipalities, and it was the Crisis Staff who went out looking for facilities or commanders of units would do it, but most likely it was the Crisis Staff who were in charge of the detention facilities. They were in charge at the time. I suppose they did it most likely together with the army because they couldn't do it on their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you misunderstand. Not to -- not the facilities. But who had actually ordered the detention of the people that were now being held in the bunker, were going to be held in the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The decision. The decision -- I precisely answered your question. Who made the decision to take people prisoner and to put them there? Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did, and the army command most likely. That's what I suppose. I mean, logically analysing how things took place on the ground, I suppose that's how it was. But I never saw any document to that effect. Nobody ever showed me that in any meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you say -- that's what I'm trying to establish, Mr. Avlijas. Did you ever ask at this meeting which were attended by members of the Crisis Staff, by Mr. Vlaco, by somebody else from the SJB as well, who has actually ordered that these people are being detained?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. There were three of us, and the main role was played by Milenko Bjelica, the court president. Now, whether he put that question to them, whether he made that request, I can't remember that now. The answer that I gave you is based on how it happened in practice. Most likely it was the Crisis Staff and the Tactical Group command that were in charge of that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: And by your leave let me clarify, because when we asked where the people, where the prisoners were from, they told us that those were people who had been taken prisoner in areas where there were armed conflicts, in Semizovac, Svrake settlement and up there in the area next to Srednja, and also in Vogosca. The residence gravitate -- the settlements gravitating towards Vogosca, Vogosca. They told us that those people had been taken prisoner during combat. That's what they told us. We didn't check whether those people were really combatants or not, but it was the corps commander who was in charge of making that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suppose the obvious question, Mr. Avlijas, is did you feel it was any part of your responsibility to establish whether people were held illegally in these conditions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. Our task was to see whether there were any prisoners and where they were kept. Now, as for the procedure our the legality and lawfulness of that issue, this is something that came under the jurisdiction of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but why did it come under the jurisdiction of the army unless they were -- happened to be captured in combat, as combatants?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We were told that those people had been taken prisoner in combat, and we told them if these are prisoners of war, then our task is this and this, to inform you of the decree of the president of the republic and to inform you of the instruction of the minister of defence, Mr. Subotic, as to how prisoners of war should be treated if you are keeping them imprisoned in your area, and we brought them Official Gazettes, et cetera. We also informed them about the situation that we found there. I reacted not only as a member of that body, of that commission, but as a normal human being, somebody who abides by the law. People are not animals. Provisions of the laws of war need to be abided by. People are people and have to be treated as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if these people in that bunker were prisoners of war captured by the army, who would be dealt with by the army, did they come under the jurisdiction of the minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, they didn't. The team that went out into the field was supposed to act on behalf of the government and Ministry of Defence and inform the Crisis Staff and the people who were in charge as to what were the instructions about what they were supposed it do on the ground. It was the government, not the Ministry of Defence that issued those regulations. And we had to inform people about how they needed to act. That was the main purpose of our mission. We did not interfere into the army affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And nobody at any stage ever told you, nor did you discover that, in fact, these people who were being held there were civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. Nobody. They claimed that those people were prisoners of war who had been captured during combat, and I told you in which areas. All the leading people of the Crisis Staff were present. President of the municipality, Mr. Koprica; president of the Executive Board Mr. Stanisic; Mr. Poplasen, the War Commissioner for Vogosca. And there were other representatives, I think representatives of the army, police and whoever else was supposed to be present was present. I even think that a representative of the army was present but I'm not sure. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just have a look, please, at another document, particularly you mentioned Dr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at 1D00-095, tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is dated the 26th of June. So was that after the meeting that you had with Dr. Poplasen and the rest of -- of the people that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. This was after our meeting, I think, and I mentioned this many times. I think that it could have been on the 11th or 12th of June. So this letter came after the meeting and our -- after we expressed our suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, if this was all a military matter, POWs and all the rest of it, do you know why in this letter Mr. Poplasen was saying: "As the prison in Vogosca who is not military is considered illegal by our legal regulations, this prison is to be immediately transformed into a department of penitentiary and correctional facility in Butmir or Pale ..."?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Professor Poplasen has a degree in political science. Most likely he didn't know these matters and did not have an advisor to explain it to him. He mixed up two different institutions here. We came looking for a facility for an investigative prison, and that was the purpose of our mission, and he probably mixed up apples and oranges if he mixed up a camp with an investigative prison. So that's not what we were looking for. We were looking for a separate prison facility so that people could be housed in appropriate conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So your take on this is he's made a mistake. All right. Let's move to -- you went to Ilijas that same --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Absolutely. This is not what we discussed, and this is not what we informed our superiors about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you never said to Mr. Poplasen or anybody else, "This is a completely illegal prison"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. We had no authority to discuss the creation of collection facilities or camps or refugee camps or whatever you want to call them. Our authority encompassed only prisoners of war. And if we found any prisoners of war, we would tell those in charge that they were duty-bound to supply normal conditions for them in compliance with the laws of war and the Geneva Conventions, without going into how they had established those facilities and so on, because that came under the jurisdiction of the Tactical Group or corps command together with the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sorry, there's one last question I keep saying we're moving to Ilijas and I always forget one last question. Planjo's house that you went to have a look at, did it -- did it -- was it, in fact, established as a prison facility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. A remand prison was established, and the inmates were transferred there. Now, as to the fate of the remand prison, I really couldn't tell you because shortly thereafter I travelled a lot. I spent a month and a half in Banja Luka dealing with exchanges, and then I moved on to Bijeljina. Now, what happened there, whether the basic court from Ilidza sent prisoners there or not, you should check with the presidents of courts who were in charge of remand prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Did the Ministry of Justice take this over from the police or whoever it was that were guarding the facility at the bunker once they were moved to Planjo's house?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: All I know is that the municipality issued a decision regarding this abandoned property, that that facility was allocated for the purposes of a remand prison. I think that that's how it was. Later on they established an investigative department, and they appointed the person to head it and other people were assigned to various other positions. The intention was to have an investigative department there -- or, rather, a department serving as a remand prison, whereas others were to be sent to Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All I want to know is are you able to tell us when the Ministry of Justice took over the control of Planjo's house?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It was in July, sometime there. I'm not sure. I did not deal with this issue later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, let's deal with Ilijas. That same day that you visited Vogosca, did you also go to Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I also attended the meeting in Ilijas. Bjelica and I went. Milorad Panjevic didn't go. We had a meeting with the Crisis Staff. The -- Ratko Adzic was the president of the Crisis Staff and the municipality and he and his associates attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any detention facilities in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. They also informed us about it, about the fact that they had prisoners there. Given the experience from Vogosca, we asked to see where they kept those people, and we went to the site and we saw that they kept those people in a warehouse of sorts. As far as I remember, it was close to the railroad between Ilijas and Podlugovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'll show you some photographs in a moment but -- which you've seen already but I just want to know this, you said: "Given the experience in Vogosca, we asked where they kept the people." What do you mean by "given the experience"? I mean discovering that they had prisoners in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I believe we spoke at cross-purposes. Having in mind what we had seen in Vogosca, since we came because of the same issue, we wanted to inform them better of the decree and instructions, and then we asked to see the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that's what I mean. Why -- why ask to see them in Ilijas but not in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In Vogosca we were in front of the facility itself. It was a terrible sight, and I was terrified of the person who threatened me. There wasn't much to see, though, people walking in front of the facility, and I know what kind of building that is. There are no conditions there. What conditions could you have in, say, a German bunker who had openings 30 X 30 centimetres in size? It was too much to see. The very idea of keeping people there, you must arrive at the -- at the conclusion that there isn't much there for anyone, and that was my reaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- you asked to see the prisoners at this warehouse. Were you taken to see the prisoners in the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, we were. People spoke to me. Since I was the public defender for that municipality, I knew some of them. We talked. They were in the warehouse, and I remember some bars on the windows. We were on the opposite side. One doesn't need much to imagine the mental framework of a prisoner. They grasp at straws. They wanted to know whether something could be done about the conditions. I -- the only thing I could tell them was that there were hints at exchanges, that they could be included, and the media was reported on the need to have a lot of people exchanged. That was the extent of my communication with them, and I suggested to them to ask for better conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you actually knew some of these people, and they knew you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Some of them probably recognised me. They knew me, but I can't say I knew them. Most people -- most workers in Ilijas knew me because I used to visit the factories there, and I was there sometimes ten times a month, and they all knew who the public defender was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Were these civilians, or were they people who had been captured in fighting with the Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It was the same in Ilijas and Vogosca. I was told that there were -- there was combat in the area of Ljesevo, just outside Podlugovi, and apparently that population was captured during combat. I don't know whether it was true or not. I was told that they had all been captured in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how many people, roughly, do you think were in this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I really can't recall off the cuff. I only know it was packed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask any of the people who'd come up to speak to you, "Is it true that you were fighting against the -- the Republika Srpska Army"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't discuss that topic with them. People asked for my help for the most part, trying to see whether they could get any better conditions. We only exchanged a few sentences. There were no long discussions. Perhaps I can clarify. At the time there were paramilitaries going around, and one needed to take care of one's own life. You never knew who was moving about such facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do you mean, sir, that you were worried that there might be paramilitaries listening to what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Not everybody tried to reason the way we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just have a look, please, at the photographs very quickly, which are at 03419.67, at tab 36. Is that the warehouse we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. This is the railway station in Podlugovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: And just across the street there is a nice cafe there called Jadran.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you identify that as the railway station, do you? And which --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And which -- at where? Sorry, yes. I've got myself slightly confused now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Can I suggest something? Yesterday during the proofing you showed me the bunker. You must have that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Because the picture you showed me for Vogosca does not tally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I may have got -- can we look just for a moment, please, at the next photograph in the binder, which is 03419.68. Right. Now, can you tell us, sir, if we can see the warehouse in that photograph at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It's not very clear. If this is the railway -- is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't -- I don't think I'm supposed to give evidence about that. I tell you what, sir, don't worry. I'll give up on photographs at the moment and come back to them tomorrow when I've slightly sorted this out a bit more clearly. Right. Don't worry, sir. We'll have a look at them tomorrow morning rather than us wasting time on it now. Now, after that visit to Vogosca and Ilijas, did you make a report to Mr. Mandic on what you had found?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Milenko Bjelica was the head of the team. He was in charge of submitting the reports, and I don't know what he did in the end. He was the court president.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you worked with Mr. Mandic. Did you either speak to him or put anything in writing to him about what -- the conditions that you had found during this trip?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I believed Milenko Bjelica would inform the minister because that was his task. I did inform them orally, though, when we briefed them on the situation in the field. However, Bjelica was the head of the team and he was duty-bound to write a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, when you say "I did inform them orally," who do you mean by "them"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Momcilo Mandic, the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the report that Mr. Bjelica had put in to Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it not standard practice then for a report to be circulated amongst the members of the inspectorate, of the people who had been doing the inspecting, before it went in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In an orderly state that would be the case, but at the time we had nothing. I'm afraid I cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You told Mr. Mandic orally about what you'd found. Did he express any view as to what needed to be done or what he was going to do in respect of that report you'd put in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: He probably reported it to the person who had ordered us to do so, and it was probably asked that people from Vogosca and elsewhere be moved to other place where there were better conditions. Shortly after our visit, those people were transferred from those bad facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that the -- the -- the bunker in Vogosca, which had so appalled you, that the man in charge was Mr. Vlaco. Now, can you have a look, please, at document which is 143 -- sorry, 1D00-339, tab 14. Now, I'm afraid it's a very bad copy of the letter.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. It's dated the 21st of July, 1992, and it's a decision, and it's Ministry of Justice with a signature. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And it's a -- it's appointing Mr. -- is says: "Blaco," but I think it's meant to be Vlaco, "from Vogosca shall be appointed warden of the detention" --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is -- it is Vlaco, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, Vlaco. So v.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Shall be appointed warden of detention department of the penal and correctional facility Butmir ... in the absence of the warden, commander of the guard shall perform the duties," blah, blah, blah. Given that he'd been in charge of this appalling place, why did you sign an appointment for him to be the warden of Butmir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We should start from the fact that we first needed to decide that a detention department be established in Vogosca. That would be under the competence of the court in Ilidza. Once the detention department was established, we had to set up personnel in charge of it. It is true that Branko Vlaco was at the bunker. However, this was not my decision. I only signed on what minister had agreed with the Crisis Staff, because the Crisis Staff had proposed him. This decision was needed for Branko Vlaco not to be mobilised to the front lines but to work for the Ministry of Justice. How did the signing of this document come about? Because Minister Mandic was not in Butmir where the ministry was. He attended a government session. Mr. Branko Vlaco came for supplies from Vogosca, and one needed to traverse 100-plus kilometres over hills in order to reach Kula. He came there. The minister was absent but he needed the decision and he needed it upon his return to have permits issued for his work obligation. The arrangement had been made with the minister, and I only had to put this in writing, and it was in keeping with all previous decisions. The minister told me that I should sign on his behalf so that Branko Vlaco would not go back empty-handed. Otherwise I was not in charge of personnel policy. I only had to follow through in terms of technicalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but -- but --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps I can add. I could have neither approved or denied issuing such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- yes. Well, let's go back to that. It's not your decision, it's Mr. Mandic's. But had you -- you told us you gave Mr. Mandic a report of your visit, an oral report of your visit to Vogosca. Did you explain that this appalling bunker place was under the control -- the man in charge was this man Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: He was probably better known than myself. Everyone knew who Vlaco was. He was in contact with the Crisis Staff. Personnel policy went along the following lines: It was basically the SR --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could please the witness slow down and be asked to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm really sorry, because I heard the words SDS. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Avlijas, you'll have to slow down a bit because the interpreter's lost it. Can you just tell us again what you said, personnel policy went along the following lines. Could you just say that again slowly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Personnel policy in the field was in the hands of the Crisis Staff and the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It's a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. -- yeah. Mr. Vlaco was, in fact, from Vogosca. Butmir, which is Kula prison - is that right? - was in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So which Crisis Staff said that they wanted Mr. Vlaco to be appointed the warden of Butmir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why should Vogosca be able to influence Mr. Mandic as to who was appointed the warden of the prison in Butmir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Something needs to be cleared up here. The correctional department established in Vogosca was an outpost. It was a part of the organisational structure of the penal correctional facility in Butmir. It was not an independent institution. It was merely a part of a larger institution which due to the conditions at the time was forced to establish such an outpost because there were very poor communication links between the court itself and the rest of the locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally on this topic, you signed this for Mr. Mandic. Was there ever an occasion if you signed a document, an official document, that you would do so without authorisation from Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: There was no way. Every document had to be registered. The stamp of the Ministry of Justice was with the secretary of Mr. Mandic. He -- the secretary was Mr. Mandic's right hand. There was basically no way, even theoretically, that such a thing would occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sticking for one last -- the last document, I think, for today, could you have a look, please, at document - sorry - P1318.33. This is a letter from -- it doesn't -- I don't -- it may have been a draft but it doesn't appear to have any signature on it, from Mr. Mandic to Vogosca, 10th of August: "Regarding your request for engagement of detainees in works, we hereby inform you that we are in agreement that detainees be temporarily engaged in construction and other works." Now, there is some handwriting on there. Are you able to -- the translator couldn't read it, but are you able to read it or recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: "Note: A discussion held with the minister on the 10th of April, 1992. Approval obtained." Signed by "Vlaco."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 10 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you recognise -- well, do you recognise Mr. Vlaco's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. I never communicated with him by way of correspondence. Therefore, I don't know what his signature looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vlaco, by August, was in charge -- or had received his appointment as warden of the correctional facility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: As warden of the correctional investigative department in Vogosca. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And therefore, if it was under the Ministry of Justice, it dealt with civilian prisoners, not prisoners of war. And when I say "civilian," I mean not people who were prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what the category of those prisoners was. I was explained that these people were captured during combat. It is a fact, though, that they were handed over for care by the command of the 1st Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the KP Dom. They had no facilities for them, and they said, "Well, it's up to you to guard them, to feed them." And the rest took place following army's approval. I don't know what Mandic had to do with this, and I'm afraid I cannot tell you anything further regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, how -- how do you know to which type of prisoner this document refers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I do know because there was no prison there. There were no convicts there. These could only have been prisoners. Under the Law on Criminal Procedure, any contact between convicts and the outside world is forbidden, and they cannot be used for any labour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence of his answer and slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time. Can I just -- I want to try and clarify this with the witness, but if Your Honours think we ought to stop, then we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The interpreters asked for the witness to repeat the last sentence, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said: "Under the Law of Criminal Procedure, any contact between convicts" that should be, not conflicts, "and the outside world is forbidden, and they cannot be used for any labour." Did you say something else after that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Detainees what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: There's a difference between detainees and convicts or those held in custody and convicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, what I'm trying to understand is this: If, as you're suggesting, because prisoners could not be put to labour, these are prisoners of war, why is Mr. Mandic involved in this at all, because he had no authority over prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It is not clear to me either. He had no authority. The prisoners in Vogosca were not supposed to be used for anything in the absence of the approval of the Tactical Group commander. I don't know what his authority was. As for the minister of justice in this part of work, he held no sway in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, if the people who were being held in this facility of which Mr. Vlaco was the warden were not, in fact, prisoners of war but people who, however they had come to be detained, were civilians, then Mr. Mandic would have had authority, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honour. I think the whole line of questioning is leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the last question I'm going to ask. He wants to answer. Perhaps he should answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, and then we take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of us dealt with the category of prisoners, people who were captured. And I'm trying to explain the three categories of people who were detained through unfortunate circumstances in places where they shouldn't have been, premises of the correctional penal facility. Those people were captured. And I agree, if they were civilians, they shouldn't have been at the camp. If they were prisoners, they probably did belong in a camp. However, Mr. Mandic, even if these were civilians, had absolutely no jurisdiction over them because they were treated by mistake as POWs. Mr. Mandic was able to have supervision only if convicts were involved, and then our department of criminal sentences would have had authority to supervise. And we would have had authority to inspect the constitutional provisions and whether they were observed according to the rules on the enforcement of sentences. Now, these people who were found there had been captured, and it needed to be clarified whether they had been captured as civilians or as combatants. I have no information about that. I was unable to find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment until tomorrow. Mr. Avlijas, I would remind you that inasmuch as you have been sworn as a witness, that you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side in this case, and in such conversations as you may have with anyone outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we resume in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
